#122274. The Metals Organization Has a Seabed Mining Production Gap That Its Pilot Has Not Closed

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1077 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

The Metals Organization Has a Seabed Mining Production Gap That Its Pilot Has Not Closed

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2022, The Metals Company (TMC) and offshore contractor Allseas recovered 3,021 wet tons of nodules from the Pacific seabed.
  • What matters between those endpoints is the operating record: sustained collection rates, marine maintenance, vessel availability and delivered tons sufficient to carry fixed costs.
  • It has been revealed that the November 12, 2026 corporate upgrade describes a phased approach: begin with an upgraded pilot collector and limited modifications to Hidden Gem, then invest in larger systems as operations develop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2022, The Metals Company (TMC) and offshore contractor Allseas recovered 3,021 wet tons of nodules from the Pacific seabed. Their integrated test system moved material up a riser stretching more than four kilometres from the ocean floor to the Hidden Gem. During production runs, the collector achieved 86.4 wet tons per hour. Four years later, TMC is discussing a million tons a year from an upgraded system and eventually 12 million tons annually across four vessels.

What matters between those endpoints is the operating record: sustained collection rates, marine maintenance, vessel availability and delivered tons sufficient to carry fixed costs. TMC has yet to demonstrate those economics.

It has been revealed that the November 12, 2026 corporate upgrade describes a phased approach: begin with an upgraded pilot collector and limited modifications to Hidden Gem, then invest in larger systems as operations develop. Phasing reduces the initial capital commitment. It also pushes the demonstration of the projected commercial production rates into the future.

In a recent development, the annual arithmetic is straightforward. At 5,000 productive hours, about 57% of a calendar year, a system collecting 200 wet tons per hour delivers one million tons. The second-year target of 1.5 million tons requires 300 tons per hour. Three million tons from one production system requires 600 tons per hour. TMC’s 2022 production-run rate of 86.4 tons per hour would deliver 432,000 tons at that utilization.

Sources indicate that the upgraded machines are expected to be different from the 2022 test collector. Their performance must be demonstrated, not assumed from the pilot. The operating gap is central to the project economics, and it grows with production ambitions.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines TMC’s production gap alongside Impossible Metals’ autonomous collection model and the investment consequences of underperforming equipment. The source assessment and fleet sensitivities are linked there.

In a recent development, A collector, a multi-kilometre hydraulic riser and a production vessel have to work together. The crawler encounters uneven ground and varying nodule coverage. The riser and pumps handle abrasive slurry. The vessel must remain on station while crews inspect, maintain and repair equipment. Offshore access and weather affect when those activities can occur.

A system can produce at its test rate and still lose the year on maintenance and interruptions. Fewer productive hours push the required hourly rate higher. Repeating a successful short production run does not establish a year’s availability, let alone multiple years of fleet productivity.

The difference matters because capital and offshore operating costs continue while production is interrupted. Ships, crews, marine maintenance equipment and financing cost money whether or not nodules are arriving on deck. Smaller annual production spreads fixed expenses over fewer tons and raises the cost of every ton recovered.

Recent findings suggest that TMC’s August 2025 prefeasibility presentation estimated offshore collection and transport at $179 per dry ton, or about $129 per wet ton under its 28% moisture assumption. Those are projections for a future system. They are not an audited cost record from continuous industrial mining. The revised first-production configuration needs its own cost data.

Sources indicate that the missing commercial evidence is a long enough operating record to estimate productive hours, rate degradation, planned and unplanned maintenance, retrieval time, replacement costs and the delivered cost per ton. Until then, moving from a pilot to a production forecast remains a major assumption.

Recent findings suggest that impossible Metals proposes to collect individual nodules with autonomous underwater vehicles rather than a tracked crawler and riser. A vehicle would descend, select nodules, fill its cargo compartment, return, undergo surface recovery, unload and prepare for another mission. Every trip must be repeated across an entire fleet.

Its September 2026 scientific trial, reported by Reuters, recovered approximately 450 grams of nodules from more than 4,000 metres depth. It demonstrated selective scientific collection. A commercial robot would have to carry vastly more material and sustain cycle times and availability that the experiment did not measure.

In a recent development, in the 2025 commercial concept examined by metallurgical specialist Lyle Trytten and me, each proposed vehicle carried 12 tons of nodules and had 18 collection arms. At one nodule every 1.5 seconds per arm and an average nodule mass of 100 grams, filling the cargo requires roughly 120,000 successful picks. With all arms continuously working, collection alone occupies approximately 2.8 hours.

The proposed complete mission cycle was four hours. Descent, ascent, searching, repositioning, failed picks, recovery, unloading, inspection and relaunch also consume time. The architecture has too many interdependent activities to fit those requirements into that cycle at the assumed performance.

According to recent reports, autonomous navigation and manipulator tests cannot substitute for evidence of an entire fleet repeatedly executing commercial missions. Increasing payload changes vehicle weight, buoyancy, energy use and recovery equipment. Faster picking leaves the surface operation and deepwater transit to be solved.

It has been revealed that our 2025 independent techno-economic assessment tested the financial effects of weaker-than-assumed robot productivity. At the illustrative $180 per dry ton nodule sales value, the model required approximately $2.52 billion in capital with the originally assumed robot throughput. Halving throughput while maintaining output increased required capital to approximately $4.51 billion.

Recent findings suggest that at a 10% discount rate, the modeled net present value moved from positive $863 million to negative $769 million. Even at two-thirds of original productivity, NPV fell to about $15 million, a negligible margin for a multibillion-dollar first-of-a-kind industrial fleet.

Sources indicate that these are scenario calculations, not actual bills or calibrated probabilities. They identify the key failure mode: more robots, recovery capacity, batteries, vessels and maintenance are needed to compensate for each production shortfall. A financial model based on high productivity can look attractive until realistic availability and turnaround times are included.

Industry observers note that TMC is further along technologically than Impossible Metals, but its future-scale production economics are also unsupported by a sustained operating record. Neither company has demonstrated the productive hours, throughput and maintenance costs needed to support its advertised commercial proposition.

Sources indicate that policymakers and investors should ask for extended end-to-end offshore operating records and audited unit economics before treating future production targets as investable output. The technology risk exists before accounting for nodule processing, metals markets, permitting or environmental liabilities.

The complete TFIE Briefing and linked assessment show the fleet calculations, technical assumptions and capital sensitivities. The remaining articles in the five-part series address processing, metals markets and American Samoa’s exposure.

📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Electric Vans — Are They The Final EV Frontier? Kia PV5.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van.
  • Industry observers note that inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner.
  • Julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van. Our brief takeaway: “Kool like a Kia.” Should keep the bean counters happy.

Industry observers note that inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner. We hoped to check out the LDV eDeliver 5 van, touted as selling for under AU$50,000. However, there was no stock to view and we ended up chatting to the dealer and then moving on to the MG U9 BEV ute. You can read about it here. And then we found the Kia PV5 delivery van.

Julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change. Since its launch in May, 496 PV5 have sold in Australia.

Sources indicate that the Kia PV5 reminded me a lot of the Renault Kangoo in both size and shape, and it is able to carry about the same payload. And the front looked like the BMW i3. The one we looked at had been sold and was awaiting a fitout as a camper van. The Norris Group Kia specialist was generous with his time and the information he shared. He has been selling the Kia EV5 for the past 5 months and delivered 5 of the vans. He sold his first one within a week of its arrival on the lot — to Ray, a driver working for Amazon.

Ray appreciated the 390 km range. My friendly sales rep tells me that this will be increased in 2027 models to 420 km. Ray was getting out of diesel and most of his questions were around charging and regen braking. Most of his trips were around the burbs and he was not intending to take the van on the highway. The Kia PV5 is a workhorse, with a passenger car feel and level of comfort. It even has electric lumbar support for the driver — great when you are spending so much time in the van delivering parcels in the lead-up to Christmas. It certainly has a lot more tech than the diesel he was trading in.

In a recent development, in fact, he was “blown away” by the standard features — the 360-degree camera, for example. “Vans are not known for their visibility.” On his return to the dealership for his first service, he commented on the smoothness of the torque: “It has no concerns going uphill.” He reported that the van felt “well planted on the road.” Ray has gotten used to trickle charging at home and has lost his range anxiety. Like most new EV drivers, once he started living and working with the vehicle, his fears vanished. The PV5 supports fast charging also for when Ray needs a boost on the road.

But what about that all-vital question of cost? Can we make the bean counters happy? The Kia PV5 retails for AU$56,000 (before on-road costs), which is about the same price as comparable diesel vans like the Ford Transit and the Toyota HiAce. Add to that the savings on fuel, the peace of mind from fuel security, and the reduced servicing and it is easy to build a business case for the Kia PV5 — cost per parcel delivery. The PV5 even comes with vehicle to load.

And it isn’t made in China! Can the PV5 replace Toyota’s HiAce? Find the answer in this video. The reviewer points out many features that make the PV5 an attractive option: the charge port is on the front. The van has lots of nooks and crannies for storage. She measures storage by capacity to fit in bottles of wine — for example, two in the glove box. There is a step provided to alight the van, aided by grab handles. More storage space is provided above the steering wheel, including a nifty phone slot. There are customizable buttons on the steering wheel to create shortcuts; for example, to the air conditioning settings. A wireless phone charger is nestled near the dash. The glovebox contains the V2L adaptor supplied with the van.

The fact that the van reverts to the lowest regen setting every time you restart the car is a little niggle. That, and there is no frunk — reducing the reviewer’s all-important need for wine storage. Full specs can be found here. Kia even gives you helpful advice on how to apply for electric vehicle subsidies (last page, bottom right). One of the pictures that caught my eye shows the PV5 as a flatbed truck.

Recent findings suggest that the PV5 was recently named 2026 International Van of the Year. It measures 4695mm long, 2255mm wide, and 1899mm tall on a 2995mm wheelbase. Range is stated as 416 km, but will of course vary with driving style and load. The battery is a 71.2kWh nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) lithium-ion battery. Kia offers a 165,000 km warranty on the battery. The van is front-wheel drive.

The PV5 has over 4 cubic metres of cargo capacity, double both that of the ID Buzz and the Tesla Model Y. Space enough for two euro pallets. There are multiple access points, with sliding doors on both sides and barn doors in the rear. The rear barn doors open to 180 degrees, and a low 419mm load height improves accessibility.

Goods being shipped are protected by padding on the rear doors and insides of the back. The PV5 can carry up to 740 kg. Tiedowns on the floor of the rear of the van help to secure cargo. There is also a power point in the back of the van. Perhaps a tradie can recharge their tools on site. No frunk for wine.

From the spec sheet: “Standard driver assist features include blind-spot collision avoidance, navigation-based adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, lane centring with hands-on detection, and parking collision avoidance assist.”.

A launch in the USA is financially difficult because of the 25% “chicken tax.” Kia builds the PV5 in South Korea and classifies it as a commercial vehicle, and it faces a 25% US import tariff on light trucks and commercial vans.

Sadly, the Kia PV5 doesn’t come in red, but only in white, grey and black. Most companies may take up the option of wrapping the van in their own livery. Overall, we were impressed with Kia PV5 and look forward to seeing more of them on the road throughout the suburbs as Australian delivery drivers move towards a bright electric future.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (616 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Laid-Off Textile Workers Ran Their Bosses' Hidden Exotics As A Museum For Two Years

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what's the coolest automotive museum you've ever seen?
  • That would be the Schlumpf collection in Mulhouse, France, specifically during the two-year period in the mid-to-late-70s when it was run by laid-off textile workers after their bosses shut their factories down and fled the country.
  • It has been revealed that now housed in the Musée National de l'Automobile in Mulhouse, the Schlumpf collection is an astounding piece of both car collecting and labor history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what's the coolest automotive museum you've ever seen? What about the most mind-blowing piece of automotive history you've ever beheld with your own eyes? I live right down the street from the National Automotive Museum in Reno, NV, which is a great time, but it doesn't quite take the cake. There are some real gems out there, like the Gilmore Car Museum, which lets you drive a Model T, or the Studebaker National Museum, where you can watch footage from 1932 of grown men throwing cars down a hill for safety testing. But if I had a time machine and could visit any car museum anywhere in time and space, there's one in particular that I'd just love to see.

That would be the Schlumpf collection in Mulhouse, France, specifically during the two-year period in the mid-to-late-70s when it was run by laid-off textile workers after their bosses shut their factories down and fled the country. Yes, the story is as wild as it sounds.

It has been revealed that now housed in the Musée National de l'Automobile in Mulhouse, the Schlumpf collection is an astounding piece of both car collecting and labor history. It began as the personal (and, sure, slightly obsessive) collection of Fritz Schlumpf, a long-time Bugatti driver who, along with his brother Hans, ran a textile business with factories in Mulhouse. Born around 1906, Fritz Schlumpf began collecting Bugattis intentionally in the 1960s. He hunted them down with the help of the British Bugatti Owners Club, who helped him locate around 50 individual cars, plus a stash of 30 vintage Bugattis owned by John W. Shakespeare of Hoffman, Illinois. Over two years, Schlumpf and Shakespeare negotiated a purchase price, bringing Schlumpf's personal Bugatti collection up to 80. Then he bought 18 more off Ettore Bugatti himself. Schlumpf was only getting started.

In a recent development, eventually, Fritz Schlumpf owned an estimated 105 Bugattis, which might've comprised as much as 20% of the Bugattis in existence at the time. Who can blame Schlumpf for apparently wanting them all? After all, Bugattis do drive like a dream, even the old ones. But Schlumpf hadn't just been buying up cars of his favorite French brand. He'd actually been amassing a mind-bogglingly large stable of rare cars, both vintage and contemporary.

By the 1970s, Schlumpf had over 400 cars stashed in an unused factory in Mulhouse that was being fitted into a museum. But in order to acquire them all during a worsening economy, he'd spent money from a government grant intended to keep his factories in operation. When his transgression was discovered, he promptly shut down all his businesses and fled to Switzerland, putting about 1,800 workers out of business.

Industry observers note that in response, the workers decided they didn't need a boss and could keep things running without Schlumpf's oversight, so they formed a workers' co-op to keep themselves employed. When members of the co-op traveled to the supposedly unused factory in Mulhouse, what they discovered was a building packed to the gills with exotic cars. A collection the likes of which had never been seen. The workers collectively decided to run the museum while using it to spread the message of their cooperative to the wider world.

The museum was open for two years, with public access to the vehicles for a few hours a day, and it contained some real stunners, including gems like two Bugatti Type 52s, which were electric race cars sized for children. You can still see the collection today, though not exactly as Schlumpf originally had it. The collection was seized by officials and eventually reopened in 1982.

Why Toyota Land Cruisers Have A Reputation For Being Nearly Indestructible

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1971, Toyota put out an ad for the Land Cruiser.
  • Recent findings suggest that even back then, the Land Cruiser was already establishing a reputation for being hard to kill.
  • So where did that legacy for toughness begin?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1971, Toyota put out an ad for the Land Cruiser. The picture was of a 12-year-old FJ25, and the headline read, "We'll know how long it lasts when the first one wears out." In the ad Toyota touts how the Land Cruiser is designed and built to last. From its steel bumper to its heavy-duty suspension to the straight-six 155-horsepower engine, everything was engineered for durability.

Recent findings suggest that even back then, the Land Cruiser was already establishing a reputation for being hard to kill. Indestructible, some might even say. Earning this title was no accident. Toyota built it from tough stock — the Land Cruiser literally used commercial-grade parts the first go-around. Once it was released into the wild, it was soon being used around the world in all sorts of harsh conditions, completing jobs that tested its mettle. Land Cruisers became known as being reliable and tough.

So where did that legacy for toughness begin? Let's look at the very first step in the Land Cruiser lineage, a prototype for the Japanese National Police Reserve. Back in 1950, Toyota needed a Jeep-sized ¼-ton four-wheel-drive vehicle built with parts local to Japan. Toyota used the chassis from the one-ton SB truck, which came with a ladder-style frame, solid front and rear axles, and leaf springs. The Type B engine came from the four-ton BM truck. Let's do some quick math here–a one-ton chassis plus a four-ton engine divided by a ¼-ton truck equals a chassis that was overkill and an engine that was understressed. Thankfully, that turned out to be a great equation and became the template for Land Cruisers to come.

In a recent development, to see how that reputation evolved, let's next take a look at the legendary Land Cruiser 40 Series, which included the iconic FJ40. Debuted in 1960, the FJ40 rode on a heavy-duty ladder-style frame to tackle high-stress and twisting forces. This was the second generation powered by the F-series engine, an inline-6 with a cast-iron block. It was built to have high torque at low rpms, keeping it understressed and reliable. That engine, incidentally, was in production 43 years before being retired, which meant it had the longest run of any Toyota engine. It became known worldwide as a reliable, durable all-terrain vehicle over its 24-year production run.

Industry observers note that toyota engineered the Land Cruiser to be tougher than its environment. The chassis and suspension were overbuilt for the vehicle, and the engine was designed to keep on going. Travel to just about any remote part of the planet, and you will still see a Land Cruiser variant being put to work. Land Cruisers have been used worldwide as farm trucks, fire trucks, and even combat platforms. They also deliver mail in the Outback in Australia, save lives as ambulances in Costa Rica, and are the vehicle of choice for aid organizations and the United Nations and the Red Cross. Land Cruisers are trusted around the world to handle these tough tasks for one reason — they consistently get the job done.

That ethos was passed down through the generation of trucks that followed. Yes, they got more comfortable, but they didn't compromise on the core promise. The understressed (and still thirsty) engines changed over the years, but the stout cast-iron block stuck around in the North American market until the 200-series arrival in 2008. The frame got boxed in 1967 and body-on-frame construction is still in place today. Solid front axles were standard until 1998 with the 100-series.

According to recent reports, throughout these measured changes over the Land Cruiser's 75-year history, there has been one other constant — the passion of Land Cruiser owners. These enthusiasts have arguably done more to contribute to building the reputation than anything else. Ask any Land Cruiser owner about their truck, and will gladly tell you how 200,000 miles is just getting broken in. As an owner of two — one at 240,000 miles and another at 284,000 miles — I can confirm. Claims of 400,000 and 500,000 miles are not unheard. This trust in their vehicles and reluctance to part with them is a good part of why Land Cruisers have such good resale value.

Recent findings suggest that those looking to get into a newly introduced Land Cruiser are in luck. In 2024, after a two-year absence, Toyota gave us the revival of the off-road icon in the form of a brand-new Land Cruiser. It comes from the Prado line of Land Cruiser, which has been upholding the Land Cruiser name and reputation worldwide since 1990. Will it be another legend? Time will tell.

#122262. Tech Report: These Are The Least Reliable Years For The Toyota RAV4

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2518 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: These Are The Least Reliable Years For The Toyota RAV4

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, since the very beginning, Toyota's RAV4 has been a no-nonsense vehicle.
  • As you may know, this pivot in the RAV4's image would handsomely pay off.
  • Industry observers note that today, we ask one further question: what are the least reliable RAV4s?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, since the very beginning, Toyota's RAV4 has been a no-nonsense vehicle. Well, kind of. The original RAV4 concept, pre-production models, and first full generation had an undeniable spunkiness thanks to their "toy car" looks and a cheeky soft-top version, which is still the best RAV4 ever made. But as soon as sales data came rolling in, showing that the practical four-door variant was selling well, the RAV4 would grow up and continue on as Toyota's champion of sober family reliability — separated from any silly distractions.

As you may know, this pivot in the RAV4's image would handsomely pay off. As one of the pioneers of the crossover segment, the compact Toyota exploded in popularity and has, over the last 30 years, become shorthand for what a modern, reliable car looks like to automotive consumers. You can't go anywhere without seeing one; trust us, we once counted 436 RAV4s on a road trip. But remember what Hannah Montana sang that one time? "Nobody's perfect." As lauded as the RAV4 is for its triumphs of transportation, it is still made up of plastic and metal parts that will fail now and then.

Industry observers note that today, we ask one further question: what are the least reliable RAV4s? It's a harsh proposition, considering the model's overall legendary dependability, but for those in the market for used crossovers, these are the truly notable conversations. Whether it's electrical problems, powertrain problems, or something else entirely, the following model years are the ones that didn't quite live up to the badge.

The second-generation RAV4, which debuted for the 2001 model year, went in a more sophisticated direction compared to early examples. But this was still the early 2000s, meaning fun stuff like a five-speed manual transmission was still on the menu. The fresh RAV4 was also slightly larger and packed a 148-horsepower 2.0-liter inline-four that could be driven through a front-wheel or all-wheel-drive system. Reviews were positive at launch, and journalists were pleased with how nearly every aspect of the Toyota had been improved from the first iteration.

In a recent development, however, after miles had been put on the latest RAV4s by their owners, a few problems began to arise. Chief among them was the engine control module (ECM), which also runs the automatic transmission and was causing unexpected warning lights and rough shifts. The very first complaints were filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) in 2001 and 2002, citing slight hesitations in acceleration, odd shifting points, and the transmission popping out of gear at low speeds.

By 2006, the transmission problems had grown to a scale that prompted Toyota to concern an official bulletin on the matter, disclosing that the ECM and its manufacturing process were at fault for the problem. Additionally, Toyota's bulletin recommended replacing the ECM on affected vehicles to prevent further gearbox issues. Importantly, there was never a recall for this issue, despite the fact that it affected several model years, as you'll soon find out.

For the 2002 model year, the initial reactions from reviewers were once again quite positive. The RAV4 still sat on the well-received updated platform and was praised for its urban utility prowess and expanding number of options, especially with the more expensive "L" package. However, as often happens, the ECM problems weren't immediately widespread enough for Toyota to completely ditch the transmission and its accompanying electronics before new model years were introduced. The result was that 2002 models inherited all the same issues that had plagued the RAV4 in 2001.

Industry observers note that if anything, from a 2026 perspective, the challenges only seemed to multiply for the 2002 RAV4. According to the NHTSA's database, the 2002 RAV4 has received 555 total complaints — over 200 more than the prior year. Of the 555, 384 complaints label the powertrain as the main issue, and of those, more than 300 identify the transmission specifically as the cause. The 2002 model year distinguishes itself from the previous year in that the transmission issues began to manifest in a slightly more intense fashion.

In a recent development, these early reports cite problems such as a loud transmission thump comparable to being rear-ended when attempting to accelerate from a stop, as well as the transmission failing to shift at all. Many more reports cite unwanted acceleration and surging at low RPM, while others describe random intermittent cuts in power. And as one could imagine, several owners were quoted for transmission repairs and rebuilds instead of a simple ECM replacement (possibly before the 2006 bulletin was released), costing folks thousands of dollars in parts and labor. There were also several instances of physical damage to the transmission due to the faulty ECM, causing more issues for those who never received the ECM replacement.

In 2006, the same year it began to deal with the transmission issues on the second-gen cars, Toyota also debuted the brand-upcoming third-gen RAV4. Gone was any five-speed manual, and in came a sleek new body, updated tech, and an optional 269-horsepower V6. This was easily the best RAV4 yet, and when equipped with the top engine and all-wheel drive, this thing was the quickest in its class by 2 seconds, and outhandled all of them, too. If you need a cherry on top, we'll point you to the 9-inch movie display for the rear passengers — a massive deal for 2006.

In a recent development, this debut model year for the third-gen, however, had a major Achilles' heel hiding in its steering column. In 2008, Toyota released a bulletin regarding many customers' reports of hearing clunking and popping from the steering system, an issue that was found to be caused by a failing steering intermediate shaft. Other complaints even mention some loss of steering control or locked steering wheels in 2006 models. This intermediate shaft issue was the most pervasive of all for the 2006 model year, according to the reported complaints in the NHTSA database.

In a recent development, there was never a recall for the steering issue; however, there was a notable recall (one of 11 recalls in total, by the way) for the rear suspension arm. After a 2012 NHTSA investigation, it was found that improper alignment practices could lead to the threaded portion of the rear suspension corroding and eventually failing or separating. The recall came that August and was reissued in 2013 and 2016, but NHTSA complaints regarding underside rust and rear suspension failures continue into the present day. Shockingly, this isn't even the worst situation from this third-gen RAV4.

Industry observers note that you may have noticed that we haven't yet mentioned the third-gen RAV4's standard engine. That's because its relevance sits mostly with the 2007 model year and one major problem. The 166-horsepower 2.4-liter 2AZ-FE engine was used in several Toyota models over the years and is known to last with proper care. But in the RAV4's case, oil consumption clouded what was otherwise a perfect package.

In a recent development, the 2007 RAV4 has the most NHTSA complaints of any model featured in this article, at an impressive 1,003 complaints. Among them, 236 cited complications with the engine or oil consumption. Years after release, when the problem began to emerge, Toyota issued another service bulletin to its dealers, teaching its technicians how to test for oil consumption and disclosing that it had redesigned the piston assembly to fix the concern (yikes). It even got to the point where Toyota had to launch a warranty extension program for qualifying vehicles (i.e., those that were tested by Toyota dealers and confirmed to have the issue).

One could make a case for the 2007 RAV4 as the worst model year ever. In addition to the oil consumption problem that took years to fix, the rear suspension and steering shaft concerns from the 2006 model were still occurring. There was even a recall for malfunctioning accessory seat-heater wiring that could cause interior fires (and two additional investigations into power-window switches that caught on fire, which also ended in a recall), on top of the hundreds of complaints in other categories. With more than 1,000 complaints, 14 recalls, and four investigations, this RAV4 may be the one to avoid.

Fast-forward to the next decade, and Toyota is releasing the all-newly introduced fourth-generation RAV4, with many changes in store. The exterior design took the model into the modern age, with a clunky and somewhat unfamiliar look compared with previous RAV4s. Additionally, Toyota eliminated the third-row seating and removed the door-mounted spare tire in favor of a floor-mounted unit. The saddest news, however, was that the powerful V6 would live no further in the RAV4, and the model would instead use just one 176-horsepower 2.5-liter engine across all trims.

Still, none of those changes are the reason for its appearance on this list. Instead, the 2013 RAV4 suffered from defects in both the torque converter and battery areas. Several early NHTSA complaints from 2013 report power surges, drivetrain jerking, stuttering, and even transmission failure in low-mileage examples. As the pool of complaints grew, Toyota eventually released a service bulletin addressing the issue, citing the transmission's torque converter as being at fault. According to the bulletin, these torque converter stuttering instances occurred in the 25 to 50 mph range and at light loads. Toyota later extended warranty coverage for the shudder on 2013 to 2015 models.

In a recent development, thirty-two torque converter complaints were sent to the NHTSA out of the 256 total complaints, but the number one glitch was the battery hold-down. Toyota disclosed that some replacement batteries have smaller tops than others and, under sharp turns, they could let the positive terminal touch the metal hold-down bracket. There was a recall for this problem in 2023, but the 2013 RAV4 still had other miscellaneous annoyances, like faulty accessory trailer-light modules.

Unsurprisingly, the 2014 RAV4 had to deal with the carryover of the 2013 model's issues, and there are a significant number of NHTSA complaints for both the battery hold-down and transmission/torque converter issues listed for this model year. But the 2014 model year saw an equal number of complaints for power steering problems and "powertrain" issues.

Sources indicate that around 2015, the NHTSA began to receive concerning reports of RAV4 steering systems experiencing changes in steering effort and causing minor electrical issues. Later on, additional reports were submitted with more intense accounts, featuring steering wheels that locked up at low speed and multiple dashboard lights flashing before the vehicle lost power steering. And while the overall number of NHTSA complaints for the 2014 RAV4 is relatively low at 198, the power steering issue was something Toyota couldn't ignore. In 2015, a recall citing "an unexpected loss of power steering [that] increases the risk of a crash" was issued. The recall details that a component of the ECU that controls the electric power steering may have been damaged during manufacturing, leading to these unexpected failures.

Recent findings suggest that but even if a 2014 RAV4 has had the recall service done, potential buyers aren't necessarily off the hook quite yet. For one, there was an infotainment screen problem that affected multiple 2012 to 2014 models of the Highlander, Prius, Avalon, 4Runner, Corolla, Tundra, Tacoma, Camry, and RAV4. Toyota released a service bulletin explaining that debris could easily get stuck between the screen and the faceplate, rendering any inputs useless. Plus, there was another recall, in addition to the power steering, trailer lights, and battery complications, that involved improperly installed accessory running boards and roof racks that could fall off while driving.

The fifth-gen Toyota RAV4 debuted for the 2019 model year and attempted to continue the hybrid-forward mantra that had been established with the first hybrid RAV4 back in 2016. Its body style was boxier and more approachable than those of its predecessors, and a 203-horsepower 2.5-liter inline-four was the standard engine, lined up next to the 219-horsepower optional hybrid powertrain, both of which would be outclassed when the 302-horsepower RAV4 Prime came slightly later. It would be misleading to say that the 2019 Toyota RAV4 wasn't desirable and well-reviewed, as it would go on to become the best-selling non-truck in 2019 (as it was in 2017 and 2018). In short, the 2019 RAV4 got a lot of things right.

Recent findings suggest that the 2019 model logged 888 NHTSA complaints, a number fairly close to that extra-problematic 2007 model's total. A significant 256 of those 888 (or about 28%) stemmed from fuel-system concerns. The NHTSA reports for these issues began in the summer of 2019, with owners experiencing random fuel cutoff while driving, abnormal auto-shutoff behavior when filling up, and lack of power (or none at all) when accelerating. The fuel pump failures were part of an issue that affected at least 32 different models across Toyota's and Lexus's lineups, and ended up with a recall that was expanded to cover the RAV4 in November 2020.

Industry observers note that the RAV4 has even more qualifications for its spot on this list, though, as there were also more than 200 NHTSA complaints relating to the engine, many of them citing failing coolant valves that ended up leaking. Additionally, a recall for an unresponsive backup camera was issued for this model, stating that certain RAV4 backup cameras failed to turn on when in reverse, increasing the risk of an accident.

In 2020, the RAV4 was once again a force to be reckoned with in the industry. For the fourth year in a row, it was the best-selling non-truck in the U.S., and in 2020 specifically, it beat the next best-selling non-truck by nearly 100,000 units. That next-best, by the way, was its direct competitor, the Honda CR-V — not an easy rival to beat. Again, the "least reliable" RAV4s are still some of the most dependable cars out there, but the 2020 model is unquestionably notable for its defects.

According to recent reports, the massive headline was engine block challenges in 2020 model-year iterations of the Lexus ES 300h, Toyota Camry, Toyota Avalon Hybrid, and Toyota RAV4 (including some hybrid variants). Manufacturing errors caused some engine blocks to be too porous, which could lead to cracking and subsequent leaks of coolant. In an NHTSA document regarding the eventual recall that was issued, it was stated that this defect could cause engine overheating, stalling, mechanical failure, and an increased risk of fire. These claims match the complaints in the NHTSA database, where 181 of the 642 total complaints cited the engine as the main issue (the largest single category for the 2020 model year).

The 2020 Toyota RAV4 also experienced several other issues, including "engine maintenance required" codes and dashboard warnings for hybrid system failures, the latter of which were sometimes evidence of corroded rear electric motor cables — an glitch that affected at least 800,000 vehicles across Toyota's lineup from model years 2019 through 2023. It's also worth mentioning that the 2020 RAV4 had two airbag-related recalls; however, it still has a five-star overall safety rating from the NHTSA.

#122260. Is the Energy Crisis Accelerating the Clean Energy Transition? 4 Takeaways from the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026

Is the Energy Crisis Accelerating the Clean Energy Transition? 4 Takeaways from the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.
  • Industry observers note that the International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security.
  • What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

Industry observers note that the International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security. The report finds that the push to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels is accelerating electrification and the shift toward domestic energy sources, including renewables. Yet electricity demand is surging, grids are struggling to keep pace, and concerns about energy security are also giving coal a longer life in some countries. The IEA warns that the pursuit of energy security alone won’t deliver the emissions reductions needed to meet global climate goals.

What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts? Nick Wayth, global director of the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, explains four key takeaways from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

According to recent reports, Q: How close will current and proposed policies get us to the COP31 pledge to raise electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035? What changes are needed to bridge the gap?

Industry observers note that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reinforced the case for electrification as a way for countries to diversify their power sources and reduce dependence on imports, improving energy security and affordability. While the world’s reliance on fossil fuels hasn’t changed substantially, there’s been a real shift in how countries think about the risks of that dependence—and the benefits of electrification. But progress is too slow. The IEA projects that under current and proposed policies, electricity will account for only 29% of final energy consumption by 2035. That’s only half the increase needed to reach the COP31 target of 35%.

It has been revealed that much of the technology is already available. The IEA estimates that nearly half of fossil fuel demand in road transport and more than a third of demand for low- and medium-temperature industrial heat could be electrified at a competitive cost today. The challenge is creating the conditions for businesses and households to make that switch.

It has been revealed that to reach the target, countries need to develop detailed intends for shifting transport, heating, and heavy industry toward electricity and invest in transmission and distribution. Governments can help keep their industries competitive by making it more attractive for businesses to switch from gas to affordable electricity. Some countries are doing this successfully already. Germany, for example, has reduced electricity taxes for manufacturers and has subsidized grid charges, helping lower electricity costs for businesses.

Sources indicate that Q: The IEA projects rapid growth in electricity demand from both air conditioning and data centers. How do the challenges posed by these two sources of demand differ?

According to recent reports, energy demand from AI and data centers has dominated public attention this year, but by 2035 the global growth in electricity demand from cooling is forecast to be about 70% greater than from data centers. Notably, the IEA finds that global demand for cooling buildings is overtaking demand for heating them for the first time in history.

Energy demand from data centers is concentrated in the U.S., China, and the EU. By contrast, demand for cooling is widespread, especially in emerging and developing economies where much of the population is vulnerable to extreme heat, an increasing threat to human life.

Under current and proposed government policies, cooling is projected to account for 12% of global electricity consumption by 2035. But during periods of peak demand, when millions of air conditioners are running at once, it could reach around 30% of the electricity needed. Electricity grids must be able to cope with these spikes in demand, even if they occur only occasionally. Without better planning and more efficient cooling, countries could face costly grid upgrades—or risk power outages during extreme heat.

Recent findings suggest that this is why policymakers and utilities need to anticipate future electricity demand and proposal investments in grid infrastructure accordingly. But building more isn’t the only solution. Governments and utilities should also invest in energy storage and other grid flexibility measures that enable them to adapt to fluctuating supply and demand as needed.

In a recent development, Q: The energy crisis is accelerating clean electrification in some countries but also encouraging greater reliance on fossil fuels in others. What does the IEA’s outlook tell us about the future of oil, coal, and gas—and the risks of investing in newly introduced fossil fuel infrastructure?

The report indicates that global oil demand is expected to level off by 2030 under current and proposed policies. The slowdown in China’s oil demand, driven largely by electric vehicle adoption, is expected to continue. Other fast-growing economies, such as India, despite electrifying transport, are nonetheless projected to increase their demand for oil.

Industry observers note that the current energy crisis is reinforcing these differences in strategy. Some countries are investing in electrification to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, while others are turning to domestic fossil fuels.

According to recent reports, the energy crisis has given coal demand a short-term boost, and the IEA now expects coal use in 2035 to be higher than it projected just a year ago. Even so, under current and proposed government policies, global coal demand is expected to fall by 14% between 2025 and 2035, driven largely by a decline in coal-fired power generation, particularly in China. But coal use in industry is projected to fall by just 5%, highlighting the challenge of reducing dependence on the fuel.

Industry observers note that countries need to be cautious about investing in infrastructure that may not be needed. The IEA estimates that about 400 billion cubic meters (bcm) of fresh liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity is under construction and could come online by 2035. Yet under current and stated government policies, export capacity could significantly exceed demand in 2035 by70 bcm. That surplus raises the risk of underused infrastructure and investments that fail to pay off.

The IEA estimates that the world will need at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines over the next decade to meet growing electricity demand and connect new sources of power, including renewables. Another 15 million kilometers of existing lines will need to be upgraded or replaced. Both will require substantial investment.

The biggest challenge is delivering these changes fast enough. Major grid projects can take 5 to15 years to plan, secure permits for, and complete—far longer than many renewable energy projects. Governments need to speed up permitting and grid connections, improve coordination between utilities and developers, and encourage investment before demand materializes. One encouraging example is the EU’s recent provisional agreement to streamline permitting for grid projects.

Equally crucial is to invest in ways to use existing assets more efficiently. Grid-enhancing technologies can speed up connections by allowing existing power lines to carry more electricity, reducing the need to build newly introduced infrastructure. And increasingly, governments and utilities are seeing the importance of making grids more flexible—building in capability and strategies to balance supply with demand in real time. Brazil, for example, pays large electricity people to temporarily reduce consumption when the grid is under strain. Businesses that fail to deliver the agreed reductions can lose payments or face suspension from programs. By combining energy storage, demand-response programs, smart grid controls, distributed energy generation, and other flexibility strategies, energy planners can meet growing demands and increase resilience while reducing the need to build more grid infrastructure.

In a recent development, courtesy of WRI. By Sarah George, Senior Manager, Strategic Communications, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition; and Francisco Boshell, Global Lead, Decarbonized Energy Consumption, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition.

In a recent development, 'Tis the season when Americans drown the last few months of hardship, like the doubled cost of car repairs and record upcoming car price highs, in gravy and egg nog and go gung-ho on buying gifts for friends and family. I tend not to partake in the yearly ritual, but if I do participate, one of my favorite gifts to give or receive is a book. Sometimes the people in your life surprise you with titles you would have never come across on your own.

The act of book-giving is actually a common practice for the Christmas Eve holiday in Iceland. "Jólabókaflóð, which translates to "Christmas Book Flood" is the practice of gifting your loved ones books on Christmas Eve. In this ever-present digital world, it's nice to be given something tangible that can be enjoyed and shared with others.

Recent findings suggest that lucky for automotive enthusiasts, there's an endless bounty of books on everything from cars to planes, to race cars and sinking ships. You name it — there's probably a book about it. So, tell us, what car-related books are you reading right now?

Thanks to my ADHD and tendency to "mood read," I have a terrible habit of starting a book, setting it down, and finishing another book instead, therefore leaving a trail of unfinished, to-be-read-later books behind. In that collection sits "Life After Cars" which I started months ago, and appear to have only finished the introduction. If you want to know more on it, Jalop Collin Woodard wrote this insightful review earlier this year. The other I truly need to finish is "Bruce McLaren, The Man and His Racing team" by Eoin S. Young. It's just shy of 200 pages of reading, so it's a light read. So far it comes off much like a parallel accompaniment to the McLaren documentary.

If I had to list the books I'm eyeing to eventually read in the near distant future, there's the coffee table book I purchased earlier this year on the Porsche 718 and 804, and also I picked up a book called "Carmageddon" which looks like it runs along similar messaging to "Life After Cars.".

Now, take a look at your bookshelf, end table, desk, or whatever odd place you find yourself leaving your books and tell us about the car-related books you've been reading. Our own magnificent fearless leader, Erin Marquis, is reading "Terror in the City of Champions: Murder, Baseball, and the Secret Society That Shocked Depression-Era Detroit." She says it's a gripping read about the heyday of Detroit covering sport, city, political, labor and automotive history.

Industry observers note that if you're not reading something that hits the spot via car, racing or anything transportation-related, is there a book you've finished recently you'd like to share with your friends here? Or is there something you purchased that calls out to you every time you pass it in the room, and you can't help but go "man, I really need to read that soon?" Bring on the book recommendations!

  • Another day, another security scare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

Industry observers note that the CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

In a recent development, meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

Industry observers note that so what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

Industry observers note that etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The manufacturer is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are currently investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In….

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal users’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

Sources indicate that but Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Sources indicate that optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and noted it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Sources indicate that crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

In a recent development, lighter remarked its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Sources indicate that traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank mentioned customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank remarked security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto firm.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

According to recent reports, crypto owners have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1474 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.
  • Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.
  • A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.

Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.

But access is only the first step. A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable. An electric irrigation pump is unlikely to raise a farmer’s income if crops can’t reach buyers. And a small business may gain little from electricity if it lacks financing to buy the equipment it needs to expand.

For energy to improve people’s lives, it must be affordable, sufficient, and reliable—and people and businesses must be able to put it to productive use.

The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) calls for “universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services” by 2030. But the two indicators used to track its universal-access target focus only on whether people have access to electricity and whether they primarily rely on clean fuels and technologies. They do not address reliability, affordability, or economic impacts.

In a recent development, other approaches already offer a fuller picture. The World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program developed the Multi-Tier Framework to measure electricity access beyond connections, including whether electricity is available when needed, adequate for the equipment people want to use, reliable and affordable. While the framework is used by some countries to assess these broader dimensions of energy access, such measures are not the default, as many countries rely on the U.N.’s official global indicators.

According to recent reports, as governments consider what should follow the SDGs after 2030, they should make multidimensional energy-access measures a regular part of national surveys and use the results to track progress globally. Since access alone does not necessarily deliver better livelihoods, improved measures of access could also be paired with indicators of whether energy is delivering the development outcomes it is intended to support. These could include whether clinics and schools can function as intended, farmers can increase yields and incomes and businesses can grow revenues and employment.

Together, these measures could shift energy planning from the largely supply-side question of how many people have access toward the demand-side questions of what people and institutions need energy for and whether the energy system enables them to meet these needs.

The examples below show why looking beyond connections matters in practice.

Industry observers note that national electrification rates can mask large differences in where electricity is available within a country. Addressing those gaps requires looking beyond national averages to identify the households, businesses, and public facilities that lack access.

It has been revealed that in 2023, WRI, working closely with Uganda’s Ministry of Health, used WRI’s Energy Access Explorer (EAE)—an online mapping tool that combines energy data with information on infrastructure, public services, and economic activity—to assess the electricity needs of health facilities. The analysis found that 675 facilities serving more than 3 million people had no electricity, either grid or off-grid, yet all were in areas with significant solar energy potential. The analysis helped identify places where solar power could fill the energy gap.

Industry observers note that in Ethiopia, the Ministry of Water and Energy and the World Bank used EAE to help design a financing program for off-grid electricity. The analysis identified 145 priority woredas, or districts, where investments could reach more than 19 million people. Having this location-based data helped translate national energy-access goals into decisions about where public financing should be directed.

In a recent development, ethiopia also illustrates why simple access figures can overstate the level of service people receive. A 2025 national energy-access survey found that 65% of households had access to at least one source of electricity. However, just 44% of the population received at least a basic level of electricity service, enough for uses such as lighting and charging a phone for at least four hours a day.

Simply having an electricity connection is not enough if the supply lacks the capacity or voltage stability to operate the equipment people need.

It has been revealed that in the Gumla district in Jharkhand, India, villages that had gained household grid connections still lacked enough power for many businesses to function. WRI found that the single-phase electricity supplied was insufficient for productive uses such as milling and oil pressing. Beginning in 2015, Mlinda Charitable Trust, a nonprofit, installed solar mini-grids that supplied three-phase electricity, allowing local enterprises to run equipment, including rice and wheat hullers, oil expellers, flour mills, and pulverizers.

Governments should assess not only whether communities are connected but also whether the electricity supplied can meet the capacity and power-quality requirements of the services and equipment people need—and plan grid upgrades or complementary systems accordingly.

In a recent development, A connection provides limited benefit if households, businesses, or public facilities cannot pay for enough energy to meet their needs. Measuring meaningful access therefore also means asking whether the energy is affordable for the people and institutions expected to use it.

Industry observers note that in Ethiopia’s Berbere district, farmers initially used petrol-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, but high fuel and maintenance costs meant these were too expensive for many to keep using. Petrol cost $91 to $203 per hectare a year, while repairs and the cost of transporting fuel added further expenses.

Industry observers note that WRI and the Danish nonprofit DanChurchAid later installed two solar-powered pumps serving 48 farming households. The solar systems have no fuel costs, while maintenance costs are less than $10 a year, compared with more than $1,300 for petrol pumps. But the two pumps’ combined $19,200 upfront cost was beyond what most farmers could afford out of pocket. Governments and funders should therefore assess both the ongoing cost of using energy and the upfront cost of the technologies needed to use it, and provide financing or targeted support where high initial costs remain a barrier.

Being connected to the grid does not mean electricity will be available whenever it is needed. WRI researchers documented power cuts lasting three to 12 hours a day at two health facilities in Jharkhand, with outages worsening during the monsoon season. The facilities relied on diesel generators and small battery backups during outages.

In 2017, after solar photovoltaic systems and larger batteries were installed, the facilities were able to keep wards and offices running and power other essential equipment during grid outages, reducing their reliance on grid electricity.

Tracking the frequency and duration of outages would give a clearer picture of whether electricity is dependable enough to support essential services.

It has been revealed that even when energy is available, adequate, affordable, and reliable, it may not translate into better livelihoods. People also need equipment, financing, and access to markets to put energy to productive use.

In Uganda, WRI Africa and partners used EAE to identify $15 million in potential investments in renewable energy technologies, including solar-powered irrigation systems and equipment for cooling and milling, that could benefit more than 28,000 farmers. Some organizations identified through that work have since secured funding for related projects. Masaka District Farmers Association, for example, received an IKI Small Grants award for an irrigation project that equipped 150 hectares of coffee-growing land with drip irrigation and worked with 1,500 smallholder farmers.

According to recent reports, in Berbere, solar-powered irrigation has enabled farmers to harvest three to four times a year and grow higher-value crops. In their first season, many farmers earned four to 10 times as much from onion, pepper, and cabbage sales as they had previously earned in a year from staple crops.

Tracking these outcomes alongside measures of energy access can help show whether investments are translating into higher productivity and incomes.

Making greater use of existing multidimensional measures, alongside complementary indicators of development outcomes, could change not just how governments report progress but also how they blueprint and direct investment.

According to recent reports, rather than starting with how many upcoming connections a project can deliver, governments and funders would ask what people and institutions need energy for, what prevents them from using it effectively, and which investments could remove those barriers. In some places, that may mean extending electricity supply. In others, it could mean improving reliability, lowering costs, or helping farmers and businesses obtain the equipment and financing needed to use energy productively.

Sources indicate that energy is essential to improving human well-being, but it is only one part of what drives development. Like water, health care or education and energy is necessary but not sufficient. Treating access as a starting point rather than an end goal—and measuring whether people can use, afford, and rely on the energy they receive—would give governments a clearer picture of whether energy investments are improving people’s lives.

Courtesy of WRI. Experts: Dimitris Mentis, Harsha Meenawat.

Every Car Brand Has To Install Seat Belts, But Wearing Them Still Isn't Universally Mandated

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buckling a seat belt is second nature, or it should be.
  • Early iterations of the seat belt were developed in the 19th century and intended for aircraft.
  • It has been revealed that in 1984, Latest York became the first state to make seat belt use mandatory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buckling a seat belt is second nature, or it should be. Once the car door is closed, next comes that click of confirmation. But safety belts were introduced long, long, long after 1769, when the first car ever made came into existence. Not that seat belts were an afterthought; they simply weren't thought of at all. Not for cars, anyway.

Early iterations of the seat belt were developed in the 19th century and intended for aircraft. Seat belts weren't added to consumer cars until 1949, when Wisconsin-based Nash Motors Organization introduced them. Still, not until 1968 were seat belts federally mandated for every seating position in passenger cars. This standard was later amended to include buses and trucks; however, this was merely a manufacturing requirement. Actual seat belt usage and enforcement were left to the states. Because of this, there remains one state that doesn't require adults to wear a seat belt: New Hampshire.

It has been revealed that in 1984, Latest York became the first state to make seat belt use mandatory. The exceptions were children who, depending on age and weight, are to be secured either in a child safety seat or booster. Keep in mind that Volvo, the maven of automotive safety, introduced the three-point seat belt in 1959. Despite evidence showing seat belts not only minimize injuries but also save lives, automotive safety systems receive plenty of pushback, at least initially.

Following New York's lead, other states enacted seat belt laws throughout the '80s and '90s. Maine was the last state to make seat belt use required, putting its law into effect in late 1995. In the decades since, New Hampshire has remained a holdout, though its nonchalance toward seat belts is strictly an adult matter, to be fair.

Recent findings suggest that all other states and the District of Columbia require front-seat occupants to buckle up. For backseat passengers, only 34 states and D.C. say it's a must. And kids being kids have different rules entirely. Some states necessitate seat belt use for front occupants only. Others require that each person be clicked in, regardless of seat location. For children, because standard seat belts cannot properly restrain them during a crash, we've got car seats, booster seats, and other safety equipment to consider.

It has been revealed that the rules in New Hampshire do account for minors, requiring occupants younger than 18, including teen drivers, to be properly fastened. There are exceptions, though. Children don't need to be buckled if they're riding in a vehicle built before 1968 (or in a bus or taxi), have a physical condition that prevents seat belt use, or fall under certain special-education conditions. Everyone else? They take the state's motto of "Live Free or Die" to heart.

Sources indicate that according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, seat belts reduce serious injuries and deaths by about 50%, and saved nearly 15,000 lives in 2017. Before seat belt use became law, only 14% of people wore them. Usage increased to 59% within a decade. In 2025, 92% of drivers and 90% of front-seat passengers buckled up, according to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety. But in New Hampshire, less than 80% of travelers bother to buckle.

Industry observers note that new Hampshire authorities are aware of this less-than-stellar safety record. The New Hampshire Office of Highway Safety (NHOHS) promotes "Join the NH Clique," which coincides with NHTSA's nationwide Click It or Ticket seat belt enforcement campaign. Law enforcement takes a no-excuses approach during the program, but they might as well be yelling at clouds from their front porch because it achieves the same effect. After all, police can't write tickets when a law hasn't been broken.

The state legislature has tried multiple times to introduce bills requiring seat belts for all, but every effort failed. A 2023 attempt was even soft-pitched as a secondary offense. Had the bill passed, actual usage would have depended on whether seat belt violations were treated as primary or secondary offenses. As of November 2026, just 35 states and D.C. have primary enforcement laws, and numbers support that reasoning. Nevertheless, whether old-timey lap belts or innovative multi-adaptive safety belts (another Volvo invention), no amount of safety tech matters unless people are compelled to wear them.

Industry observers note that the National Safety Council (NSC) compiled NHTSA data from 2024 that revealed seat belt usage at 91.2%, yet unbuckled occupants accounted for 48.4% of passenger vehicle deaths. Among 21- to 34-year-olds, about 60% of occupants killed weren't buckled. The NSC notes that in California — where seat belt use is a primary-enforced law for everyone aged 16 and up – observed usage in the front seats was 97.5% and unrestrained occupants accounted for 43% of occupant deaths. North Dakota, which only switched to primary enforcement in 2023, saw 79.8% usage while unbelted occupants accounted for 53% of deaths. The statistics from New Hampshire are more somber, showing only 78.2% wear their belts, while unbelted occupants accounted for 59% of deaths.
