Recent findings suggest that before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was debuted in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it notes. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to customers, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

According to recent reports, schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ford is now a battery producer. Yes, it’s using battery technology licensed from CATL, but it is now producing EV batteries it is going to be using in its own vehicles. In fact, it is reportedly doing so in a really fast, advanced way. “The BlueOval Battery Park Michigan assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.2 That pace helps drive down battery costs, and the facility has capacity for more. But speed must go hand in hand with quality,” Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, writes.

According to recent reports, “The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes. With this milestone, Ford is now in the battery business and will be the first to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer automotive use,” Poon writes. He goes on to explain further in a recent article why Ford chose to produce LFP battery cells and a bit on how it is doing so. Here’s a bit more from that article:.

According to recent reports, “The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule. Ford now delivers cells at a plant it owns and operates, building expertise to support more affordable electric vehicles (EVs) and Ford Energy’s battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

“Why Start with LFP Prismatic for Fathom?

Sources indicate that “When Alan Clarke, vice president, Advanced Development Projects, first joined the development team that created the Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, he issued a clear challenge: find an efficient LFP prismatic battery. The goal was to make EVs significantly more affordable.

Recent findings suggest that “We talked to battery companies around the world. We wanted a technology that was proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale, and suited to what we were building. That led us to the world’s leading battery manufacturer, CATL, whose batteries power 30 million vehicles across the globe.

It has been revealed that “A battery is one of the biggest contributors to an EV’s cost and weight. So, we asked: How do we get more out of the battery without simply adding more cells? Our answer was efficiency over excess.

According to recent reports, “LFP chemistry uses no nickel or cobalt, which helps hold down costs. It also holds up over years of charging and use. That durability is valuable as we give customers ways to use their battery beyond driving. For example, AC bidirectional power lets a vehicle receive electricity from a properly equipped home and supply power back to it.1.

“This milestone is about more than shipping our first cells. We’re building the expertise to produce high-quality batteries at scale — for more affordable EVs and a newly introduced energy storage business.”.

It looks like a serious effort and serious progress toward making more affordable, more competitive electric cars at Ford. The aim has been to get as good as making electric cars as Chinese companies are. How effective and successful will this newly introduced path be for Ford? We’ll see.

#122212. 8 Things Your iPhone Does As You Flip Your Car Down An Embankment

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2090 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

8 Things Your iPhone Does As You Flip Your Car Down An Embankment

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A phone puts in a lot of work while we're driving around, especially if your car's infotainment system is painfully old and it's doing double duty there.
  • Apple introduced Crash Detection with the iPhone 14 in 2022 (it works on iPhone 14 or later running iOS 16 or later).
  • It's worth noting that nothing here is exclusive to Apple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A phone puts in a lot of work while we're driving around, especially if your car's infotainment system is painfully old and it's doing double duty there. And while plenty has been said about how our phones can help cause a crash – texting-while-driving bans exist in every state but one – we don't talk as much about how they can be downright heroic when one actually occurs.

Apple introduced Crash Detection with the iPhone 14 in 2022 (it works on iPhone 14 or later running iOS 16 or later). The underlying technology unlocks a number of possibilities, some of which could literally save a user's life. That's because once your phone knows you've been in a crash, it can do a number of phone-based tasks that you might no longer be in a position to do yourself, from calling 911 and letting them know where to find you to alerting your emergency contacts that something has gone awry.

It's worth noting that nothing here is exclusive to Apple. In fact, Google Pixel phones have been doing crash detection since 2019. But since more Americans use iPhones than every other competing device combined, getting Crash Detection into iOS represented the first mainstream on-by-default introduction of the technology in the United States, even if many users were unaware it was even there. So if you have a different device, there's a chance it can do what's being discussed today. We're sharing the iPhone perspective for the sake of being relevant to the most users and letting us be specific about the details. So here's what your phone might get up to right after you overcorrect from hitting inexplicable gravel on that backroad sweeper.

Your iPhone starts determining that you're in a crash based on a bunch of real-time data that it's taking in all the time — think change in speed, impact force, and even changes in air pressure. But before it takes any action that could lead to a rescue helicopter being summoned to your location or scaring the daylights out of your emergency contact, it's going to evaluate whether you've actually been traveling along in a car versus, say, knocking your phone off a balcony or falling down a flight of stairs.

There are no exact criteria that answer this question. A crash detection algorithm notes things like whether you are connected to a vehicle via Bluetooth, how rapidly it is passing through the range of nearby Wi-Fi connections, and even analyzes ambient engine sounds or road noise. The goal is to cobble together a clear enough picture of what's going on to distinguish between a phone being dropped on a moving subway and one flying through the air in an auto accident. It's an approach that had to be dialed in. When the feature was first introduced, there was a tendency for crash detection to be triggered in non-crash events, such as violent jostling on a roller coaster. Subsequent updates refined the criteria, aiming to reduce false positives and emergency crews being dispatched to amusement parks.

Apple has done research with crash labs to effectively draw this line, both determining when someone is traveling in a car and also filtering out minor incidents like a small fender bender or a phone simply being knocked on the floor while a vehicle is in motion.

Once your iPhone has established that you're likely traveling in a vehicle and not bungee jumping or getting your clock cleaned playing football, it uses on-device hardware to get a handle on how much trauma the laws of physics are putting on the phone and, by extension, probably you.

Latest motion sensors introduced with the iPhone 14 include a three-axis gyroscope and high-g force accelerometer able to detect up to 256 Gs of force, which helps estimate if whatever is happening to you would land in a sufficiently severe place on something called the Maximum Abbreviated Injury Scale (MAIS). Apple notes it has set the crash detection threshold in an effort to detect incidents with a MAIS level 3 and higher, at which point your injuries are likely to include "major lacerations, multiple fractures, crushed limbs, and bruised organs." Like we said: not a fender bender.

Sources indicate that these sensors fire off more than 3,000 times per second, slowing your terrifying automotive mishap into a veritable eternity of data that captures the initial impact and every twist, turn, bump, and smash that follows. On the plus side, in this case your phone probably isn't spreading your information to advertisers, so there's that.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to cutting-edge tech like the gyroscope and accelerometer, the iPhone also leans on pre-existing hardware to decide if the thing you're experiencing is indeed a crash that warrants an emergency response. One of those is the microphone, which can capture the acoustic data needed to identify crash sounds and help distinguish a real crash from false alarms G-force data might trigger.

Industry observers note that perhaps even more unexpected than your phone listening for tire-screeching and tree-hitting sounds is what's going on with its internal barometer, a sensor used primarily to measure elevation changes for activity tracking and support location services. Because airbags have a lot more going on than you might think and can temporarily alter the ambient air pressure inside the car when they go off, that barometer can often recognize the clue and relay the data point to the algorithm for consideration.

Recent findings suggest that none of this is a sure thing. If your windows are down, the barometer might not be able to detect the change in pressure and the sounds of the accident may or may not align with what Apple's programming has decided a crash sounds like. Similar to the logic that determined you were in a car in the first place, it takes a number of differently-weighted data points to come up with an educated assessment of the situation. That assessment may be wrong, in either direction.

And because all these calculations can be wrong in either direction, the iPhone does provide a couple of clear opportunities for you to indicate there's been a wacky misunderstanding rather than a dangerous crash before it mobilizes a dramatic and potentially expensive emergency response on your behalf.

Sources indicate that before springing into action, it'll first sound an audible alarm and show an alert on the screen. This lasts 10 seconds. If you swipe where indicated it will call emergency services and if you dismiss the alert it'll cancel the whole thing. Of course, emergencies being emergencies, you might not be able to do either, in which case a 30-second countdown will occur before it moves forward.

During this time your phone will be making loud noises you probably haven't heard before, vibrating in a way you didn't realize it was capable of, and activating an LED strobe. If you swipe to call emergency services, you'll be connected. If you take no action, presumably because you can't, not because you didn't notice the air raid warnings coming from your phone, the countdown reaches zero and the phone springs into action on your behalf.

If you didn't have the foresight to sail your car into a ravine someplace with respectable cell phone coverage, you might think that all of this would just result in you having to listen to your phone make awful noises while you try to get yourself out of a dangerous situation with a cheap seatbelt cutter tool followed by it realizing it doesn't have any service anyway.

According to recent reports, not so! Since 2022, iPhone users in the U.S. and Canada with iPhone 14 models and later have had access to Emergency SOS via satellite. Whether you swiped right during the scary countdown or allowed it to reach zero while unresponsive or otherwise indisposed, the phone can use a data connection via satellite to reach help if cell service isn't available. If you're in a position to operate the phone, this won't be a voice call. You start with an emergency text, which will connect to emergency services after you enter "Report Emergency" mode. This prompts you to describe your situation using multiple choice questions to narrow down your predicament and relay the appropriate information.

Depending on where you are, a satellite connection may or may not be readily available. Dense tree cover above or the fact that you're upside down under a car may limit your phone's ability to reach a satellite. If that turns out to be an issue, the screen will walk you through how to best get a connection, such as moving to a place with a clear view of the horizon, which hopefully you'll be in a position to do. Of course, having to get yourself to the top of a hill remains preferable to having to get yourself to the nearest town.

If you have cell service, none of that satellite business happens. After you don't respond in time and the countdown reaches zero, the iPhone calls emergency services. Because you're presumably unavailable at this point, once emergency dispatch answers the call, they will hear a repeating audio message indicating that a serious car crash has been detected with an unresponsive person in need of help. The message also includes a search radius based on your approximate latitude and longitude.

Industry observers note that during this time, two-way audio is enabled and the repeating recording will play at a reduced volume, so if you become able to speak with emergency services or someone else arrives on the scene, the conversation can proceed like any other 911 call. The phone screen will be commandeered with a "Crash Detected" message and the available interface will include one button to stop replaying the recorded message and another to end the call.

By the way, this all works over Wi-Fi calling as well, so you've also got options if you happen to flip your car down an embankment and into a Starbucks or something.

After your phone is done contacting emergency services, it can also send a message to your designated emergency contacts, letting them know that a crash has been detected and that 911 has been called. It will include an approximate location. This will appear as a text message coming from you, and its content will make it immediately apparent that something significant is happening.

This only works if you've set your phone up for emergency contacts, which you do somewhat unintuitively through the Health app. Apple explains how to do it on its support page, and now is as good a time as any to get that taken care of if you haven't already. While you're in there, you can also enter any medical information that emergency responders might benefit from having, which they can access under your phone's Medical ID feature.

Recent findings suggest that don't assume that you've designated your emergency contact just because your phone seems to already know who your mom is and reminds you to call her on her birthday. You can add more than one — just make sure that whoever you put in there is someone you're willing to wake up in the middle of the night with a terrifying text message they can never unsee.

One of the most important takeaways here has nothing to do with satellite technology or crash identification algorithms. Car crashes are chaotic, and even as your phone is processing data with mind-bending speed and preparing to summon help if you need it, the device itself may also be flying somewhere you aren't going to be able to get it. This doesn't just matter because an unsecured phone can become a projectile that hurts you or someone else. It's also important because something simple like placing a call is trivial while you're driving along but can become impossible in an emergency. And the remarkable thing is that, provided your phone survives and detects the crash, it can still call for help without you ever laying a finger on it.

In a recent development, you might have no earthly idea where the phone went when you need it. The screen might be shattered and your pleas to Siri might be met with "Here's 'Help!' by The Beatles on Apple Music." Crash Detection isn't foolproof, it can't detect every wreck, and your phone might fall off your motorcycle and tell your family you crashed. On the other hand, it just might save the day.

Memo To Musk: Denial Is Just The First Step On The Long Road To Recovery

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tesla CEO Elon Musk made headlines yet again last week, when he publicly denied any affiliation with US President Donald Trump’s “MAGA” movement.
  • During an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit last week, Elon Musk claimed that he was not affiliated with MAGA, though he did not apologize for supporting MAGA candidates this year, or for supporting Donald Trump in 2024.
  • Industry observers note that in the same interview, Musk insisted — falsely — that Russia was the aggrieved party when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded the Donbas region of Ukraine back in 2014.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tesla CEO Elon Musk made headlines yet again last week, when he publicly denied any affiliation with US President Donald Trump’s “MAGA” movement. If Musk intends to stage a sort of political recovery, he still has a long way to go. Denial is just a precursor to recovery, which begins in earnest when you stop denying the reality of your situation and start admitting you need help from a higher power or some such. And in fact, a higher power is coming for Musk —  if not in spiritual form, then in the form of Congress, where the incoming Democratic majority prepares to exercise its authority, and call Musk to account for manipulating SpaceX satellite services in Ukraine.

During an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit last week, Elon Musk claimed that he was not affiliated with MAGA, though he did not apologize for supporting MAGA candidates this year, or for supporting Donald Trump in 2024. Musk simply noted he “felt foolish” for wasting his money on losers.

Industry observers note that in the same interview, Musk insisted — falsely — that Russia was the aggrieved party when Russian President Vladimir Putin invaded the Donbas region of Ukraine back in 2014. Justin sayin’….

For those of you wondering why Elon Musk’s politics should be a matter of concern to CleanTechnica, that’s a good question, and here’s the answer: Elon Musk sailed into clean tech history on the coattails of the EV startup Tesla Motors (soon to become simply Tesla) in the early 2000’s, only to emerge in more recent years as a champion of the far right alongside President Donald Trump’s notoriously racist, fossil fuel-supporting “Make America Great Again” movement, thereby setting back the US decarbonization movement by years if not decades.

Musk has also made his own contribution to the resurgence of fossil fuels in the US. His latest xAI data centers are well known for deploying loosely regulated (or illegal) on-site gas generators, and his SpaceX venture has been gobbling up natural gas for rocket fuel while laying aims for future expansion.

So much for Elon Musk’s footprint on the US energy profile. Let’s move over to Ukraine, where rich fossil energy and mineral resources in the nation’s Donbas region prompted Russian President Putin to send unmarked soldiers — aka the “little green men” — to annex that portion of Ukraine in 2014. A ceasefire temporarily calmed the situation until February of 2022, when Putin sent a fully equipped convoy to the Ukrainian capital city Kyiv, aiming to take over the entire seat of government in one fell swoop — literally, in one day.

The effort failed, both militarily and in terms of Putin’s energy goals. Ukraine promptly cut Russia off from its electricity grid and hooked up with the European grid, a complex effort assisted by the Biden administration. Ukraine also set the wheels in motion to join the European Union as a significant source of clean energy, including green hydrogen gas alongside its copious potential for clean power including biomass, wind, and solar power.

To put that into perspective, consider that Ukraine is almost 90% as large as Texas, which has staked out a leadership position in wind and solar power among the 50 US states.

With Ukraine as a leading renewable energy supplier, the EU would have a fresh opportunity to meets its decarbonization goals on schedule while also reducing imports of fossil energy from Russia… And… Well… That’s where Elon Musk enters the picture.

Musk first emerged as a full blown MAGA supporter in 2020, when he helped Trump stir up conspiracy theories and confusion over the federal response to the COVID-19 crisis, in a failed effort to support the President’s bid for re-election that year. Had Trump won, he would have continued to implement a key part of his foreign policy agenda, namely, withdrawing the US from NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Alliance. NATO formed in 1949 as an effort to curb Russian expansion in Europe, an effort Trump has upended on account of his longstanding friendship with Putin.

The election of Joe Biden in 2020 did not prevent Musk from providing additional aid and comfort to Trump. Musk used his media-grabbing public profile to undercut the authority of President Biden at every opportunity, including on the world stage as well as here at home. The stream of insults extended into January of 2022, even as the reality of a fresh round of Russian expansion into Europe began to materialize.

Musk had an additional opportunity to challenge Biden’s authority in January of 2022, when the so-called “Freedom Convoy” of truckers barricaded government offices in Canada, ostensibly in protest of a vaccine mandate. Musk gleefully cheered the effort, which disrupted transportation systems and distracted public attention in two key NATO allies — Canada and the US — even as Russia began ratcheting up its plans to take over Kyiv.

It has been revealed that however, once it became clear that Putin’s one-day takeover of Ukraine was a failure, Musk about-faced. He took credit for providing “free” communications aid to Ukraine in the form of satellite services through the Starlink branch of SpaceX.

According to recent reports, JK! A later assessment revealed that other sources shouldered about 85% of the cost of Starlink terminals initially supplied to Ukraine, including USAID here in the US (not a typo — that’s the US Administration for International Development, the same agency that Musk later destroyed in 2025).

Poland and other groups also contributed initial assistance to purchase  the terminals alongside an estimated 30% of connectivity costs. In addition, by September of 2022 Musk was making the case for US taxpayers to foot the bill.

Recent findings suggest that don’t just take my word for it. In 2023, the Belfer Center for International Affairs at Harvard recapped SpaceX’s negotiations over payment for its services to Ukraine during the previous year, concluding that “we can assume the U.S. government agreed to pay some, if not all, of the costs for continued operation of the technology.”.

“SpaceX, and particularly Musk, was able to play the role of wartime hero, showcasing the power and value of the technology products the company developed, while simultaneously avoiding sustained and hefty bills,” Belfer Center observed.

US Department of Defense contract or not, by 2023 SpaceX was already making unilateral decisions that restricted Ukraine’s ability to deploy the technology, with SpaceX CEO Gwynne Shotwell publicly insisting that the organization never intended for Ukraine to use it “for offensive purposes.”.

It has been revealed that of course, “offensive” is in the eye of the beholder. Since Ukraine is the invaded party seeking to assert its rights over internationally recognized borders against Russia, one could argue that every action Ukraine takes is a defensive one until Putin agrees to concede defeat and cede back his illegal claims over Ukrainian lands.

According to recent reports, of course, that’s not how Musk portrayed the situation in his DealBook interview last week. Nevertheless, one also could argue that the US government, not the vendor, controls the use of contractually obligated resources. Be that as it may, Musk raised the bar considerably in October, when he — or Trump — or both — once again dialed down satellite service in Ukraine, exposing that country to further attacks.

Musk attempted to mollify bipartisan outrage over the debacle with yet another publicity stunt for SpaceX. However, service interruptions have continued into this week. Meanwhile, Trump has spent the same week cozying up to both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, aided and abetted by an obedient Republican majority in Congress.

In a recent development, that majority will evaporate, though, in January 3, which is just around the corner. The incoming Democratic majority is already gearing up for a fight. In a letter dated November 20, the incoming Chair of the House Intelligence Committee, Jim Himes (D-CT), demanded an in-person briefing from senior SpaceX officers, seeking an explanation for the disruption of military-grade Starshield service in Ukraine. As leverage, Himes warned Musk that a Democratic majority in Congress will do what the Republican majority failed to do, namely, exercise its constitutional authority over federal contracts.

It has been revealed that referring specifically to SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield satellite services in Ukraine, Himes warned Musk that his entire suite of present and future SpaceX security contracts with the US government is at risk. “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes explained.

“For that reason, it is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX- developed, government-owned systems until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes continued.

It has been revealed that will Musk simply ignore the request for a briefing? After all, as Himes notes, Musk failed to respond to earlier requests. Stay tuned….

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sure, the 2027 Chevy Express is the same as the 2026 model, which was the same as the 2025, which was the same as the 2024, and so on.
  • Of course, Morgan cars have remained true to their original 1930s vibes in a lot of ways, right down to their appearance.
  • It has been revealed that morgan's long-running steel chassis was likewise fairly old-fashioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sure, the 2027 Chevy Express is the same as the 2026 model, which was the same as the 2025, which was the same as the 2024, and so on. But all joking aside, the Bowtie brand's body-on-frame van has only been riding on the same platform for about three decades. That's nothing compared to what Morgan did with its sports cars. The organization introduced a steel ladder-style chassis with its 1936 Morgan 4-4, and from that point through 2020 — a span of 84 years — nearly every four-wheeled Morgan featured the same basic setup.

Of course, Morgan cars have remained true to their original 1930s vibes in a lot of ways, right down to their appearance. Even the latest Morgan Supersport 400, the firm's most powerful vintage-look roadster yet, maintains its flowing pontoon-style fenders, ash-wood body frame, and disdain for most modern technologies. Despite being the first Morgan to come with hands-free calling, the Supersport doesn't have a touchscreen — just a small and simple driver display with a trip computer and a digital speedometer. As for advanced driver-assistance systems, well, the car doesn't even have a rearview camera. It's exempt from most federal safety regulations due to its highly limited production numbers. The company produced approximately 35,000 steel-chassis cars before switching to a new platform, representing an average of roughly 417 cars per year.

It has been revealed that morgan's long-running steel chassis was likewise fairly old-fashioned. Essentially just a pair of Z-shaped steel rails connected to each other by five cross-members, the chassis rode on a basic leaf-spring suspension at the back and a sliding-pillar configuration up front. And the roots of that front suspension go back even further, as it was developed by Henry Frederick Stanley (HFS) Morgan in 1910.

Just to be clear, Morgan actually started using aluminum chassis in 2000, when it introduced one for its relatively short-lived line of Aero cars — starting with the Aero 8, which also stands out as the first Morgan model with a BMW powertrain. However, other Morgans continued to ride on the steel setup through 2020.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Morgan was ready to introduce its newly introduced CX platform made from bonded aluminum. It first underpinned the 2019 Morgan Plus Six, which was named for its BMW-sourced I6 turbo engine. The lightweight chassis weighed a mere 220 pounds, but it was so stiff that the Plus Six had twice the torsional rigidity of the car it replaced in the Morgan lineup.

Then, in 2025, Morgan premiered the newly introduced Supersport with a further evolution of the CX chassis. The Supersport's CXV setup stiffened the chassis by 10%, plus another 10% when the detachable hardtop was in place, and enabled Morgan to enhance the steering and suspension systems as well. As regards the former, the results included a 13% quicker steering speed backed by improved feedback for the driver. The new suspension, now with standard anti-roll bars and revised geometry, promises "a compliant ride, better body control, and enhanced handling.".

Recent findings suggest that and yes, the Morgan Supersport is available in the U.S. The one major catch, though, is that we only get the four-cylinder model — a 2.0-liter TwinPower turbo-four with 255 horses and 258 pound-feet of torque. It's plenty peppy for a car weighing around 2,500 pounds. But the European Supersport 400 can deliver up to 402 horsepower from its turbocharged 3.0-liter BMW straight-six, taking the Morgan experience to a whole new level.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NRDC resources on insurance affordability, market availability, climate risk, resilience investments, and strategies to protect homeowners, businesses, and communities.

Industry observers note that for property owners, insurance provides a critical financial safety net that protects homes, businesses, and other assets from unexpected losses, helping owners recover and rebuild when disasters occur. Beyond individual protection, insurance is fundamental to the resilience of communities and local economies, enabling faster recovery, supporting continued investment, and reducing the long-term financial impacts of shocks. As risks become more frequent, severe, and costly, access to affordable, available, and reliable insurance is increasingly essential, not only for safeguarding property owners but also for maintaining overall property affordability, economic stability, and the resilience and prosperity of the communities in which they live and operate.

Sources indicate that the frequency and severity of losses are increasing faster than insurers can sustainably price and absorb them, leading to higher premiums, reduced coverage availability, and, in some cases, the withdrawal of insurers from certain markets. This trend is eroding the affordability and accessibility of insurance, increasing the total cost of property ownership, and placing additional pressure on housing and business affordability while leaving individuals, businesses, and communities more physically and financially exposed.

However, the insurance sector is increasingly recognized as a key component of resilience, incentivizing risk reduction through pricing and support for adaptation measures that can help moderate long-term insurance costs. When functioning effectively, insurance enables communities to not only recover from shocks but also to better prepare for future risks while preserving access to coverage.

Linked below are reports, expert blogs, and other resources that examine the insurability crisis and how insurance can play a key role in advancing housing resilience and adaptation.

NRDC’s director of insurance and financial risk, Alfonso Pating, breaks down how homeowner’s insurance works and why climate change is making it unaffordable.

#122201. RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies.
  • It has been revealed that I have been challenging this tension since January 2024.
  • Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies. That makes the gaps between its findings and its recommendations harder to excuse. Its latest work acknowledges that battery trucks generally have better economics than hydrogen fuel-cell trucks, that Europe needs far less hydrogen in 2030 than it originally targeted, and that low-emissions ammonia still costs substantially more than conventional ammonia. Several recommendations still seek public money to develop the very hydrogen markets the research has found difficult to justify.

It has been revealed that I have been challenging this tension since January 2024. RMI matters because governments, investors and industrial companies use its research when deciding where to spend money. Its hydrogen program has made genuine analytical corrections. It has not made all of the accompanying strategic decisions.

Consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India. The baseline comparisons find that fuel-cell trucks do not reach battery-electric truck ownership-cost parity through 2040, including the long-haul use case. The report also explores a much more favourable hydrogen price in an alternative sensitivity, which brings fuel-cell trucks closer to parity. Those are different findings, and the baseline matters to investment decisions today.

Recent findings suggest that the report nevertheless recommends hydrogen vehicle subsidies, support for refuelling stations, production incentives and tax relief. It treats a parallel hydrogen-truck market as something to build. The case for spending public money on that market should start with evidence that a particular freight service cannot be served as well or better by batteries. The reported cost advantage of batteries does not disappear when the policy section begins.

In a recent development, the problem reaches beyond India. RMI’s 2025 US hydrogen report says battery trucks have greater market readiness and lower total cost of ownership, especially in the near term, yet calls for hydrogen distribution and refuelling infrastructure along freight corridors. The independent NACFE Run on Less ownership-cost work, developed within RMI’s freight research ecosystem, projects batteries becoming the lowest-cost option across its modelled duty cycles by 2035 without incentives. Hydrogen remains the most expensive option across nearly all of them. These findings support battery infrastructure as the default and a high evidentiary bar for hydrogen exceptions.

Industry observers note that RMI already knows how to make appropriate distinctions elsewhere. Its 2026 steel research separates hydrogen used to reduce iron ore from hydrogen burned merely to supply process heat. In the illustrative plant, electric heat requires about 850 GWh a year, compared with 1,300 GWh of electricity to produce enough additional hydrogen for heating. That is the kind of direct service comparison that ought to govern recommendations throughout the organization.

Its newly introduced Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance also has a coherent industrial purpose. Fertiliser production already requires ammonia, commonly made with fossil-derived hydrogen. Purchasing lower-emissions ammonia to replace that supply addresses an existing industrial input. It does not require inventing a new energy market for ammonia combustion.

Europe shows how improved diagnosis can coexist with excessive policy ambition. RMI’s March 2025 recalibration reduced expected mandate-driven renewable hydrogen demand in 2030 to 2.2–2.8 million tons, far below the EU’s original 20-million-ton supply-and-import ambition. Its analysis identifies €13.9 billion in public support under existing mandates, plus €31.7 billion for an accelerated scenario. The combined €45.6 billion deserves a comparison with the other ways industry could obtain the same low-carbon products and services, including direct electrification and imported green materials.

That comparison changes the question for ammonia, steel and refining. A European fertiliser or chemical manufacturer needs ammonia, not necessarily hydrogen manufactured inside Europe. A steelmaker needs iron meeting its grade and emissions requirements. A mill needs process heat at specified temperatures. Governments can pay a premium to preserve domestic capacity for security or resilience, but the benefit must be valued and the public cost made explicit.

My November 2026 European hydrogen assessment applies that approach. In its central 2050 scenario, ammonia produced in Europe with on-site green hydrogen costs approximately €1,222 per ton. Qualifying imported green ammonia costs €745–755 per ton under the model’s assumptions. These are modelled values, not supplier bids. They demonstrate why an analysis that starts with hydrogen production targets can produce the wrong infrastructure strategy.

Recent findings suggest that RMI’s 2026 China green ammonia and methanol report acknowledges that green production costs remain two to three times conventional costs and that demand development lags supply ambitions. The report nevertheless discusses expanding ammonia and methanol as energy carriers, including ammonia for electricity. The relevant comparison for electricity is renewable generation with storage and other flexibility, not fossil-derived ammonia alone. RMI has not demonstrated that adding an ammonia combustion pathway wins that comparison.

Industry observers note that this is a strategy problem as much as a modelling problem. Using Richard Rumelt’s framework, RMI’s diagnosis has improved, its guiding policy remains too committed to expanding hydrogen markets, and some coherent actions are missing. An economically unfavourable comparison should be able to end an infrastructure recommendation. Instead, it too often generates proposals for subsidies that would make the hydrogen route easier to sell.

Sources indicate that RMI has the expertise to correct this. Its hydrogen recommendations should carry explicit alternative-technology comparisons, investment thresholds and exit criteria. Cross-program review should include the researchers measuring battery costs, industrial electrification, freight operations and grid flexibility. Where hydrogen is an essential chemical input or demonstrably the best means of delivering a service, support it. Where competing technologies win on cost and deployment readiness, stop trying to create demand through policy.

Sources indicate that the full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines RMI’s US, India, Europe and China reports side by side, including the differences between its findings and recommendations. It also links the original sources and the 2024 critique.

AI’s next build-out: Inference racks that resize themselves for every new model

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Memory pooling is fast becoming one of the sharpest tools in AI inference economics, with companies racing to wring more output from every graphics processing unit.
  • In a recent development, most AI servers still ship with a fixed GPU-to-memory ratio that holds for the life of the machine.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Our core fundamental technology is around pooling and sharing the most critical resources in the data center, which are now GPU and memory,” Puri mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:43 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Memory pooling is fast becoming one of the sharpest tools in AI inference economics, with companies racing to wring more output from every graphics processing unit.

In a recent development, most AI servers still ship with a fixed GPU-to-memory ratio that holds for the life of the machine. But that is a poor fit when nobody knows what model they will deploy six months from now, according to Sumit Puri (pictured), co-founder and chief technical officer of Liqid Inc.

Recent findings suggest that “Our core fundamental technology is around pooling and sharing the most critical resources in the data center, which are now GPU and memory,” Puri mentioned. “Rather than statically deploying these things inside of a server, our vision is simple. Let’s put pools of resources in the rack, GPUs and memory, and dynamically assign them to any server that needs it based upon the model or the workload that we are looking to deploy.”.

Puri spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed pooling GPUs and memory, the tokenomics of AI inference and Liqid as a Service. (* Disclosure below.).

Liqid measures payoff in tokenomics, with the yardsticks being tokens per second, tokens per watt and, above all, tokens per dollar. Supply is another pressure point in the AI infrastructure build-out, with memory among its most constrained components. But delivering only the memory each application needs stretches scarce supply further, Puri explained.

“Supply chain is a massive constraint for all of us — memory being a giantly massive constrained thing,” he said. “If we can do things like pool memory, share memory, optimally deliver memory to the server in the right amount of memory as required by the application, we can directly address some of those supply chain problems.”.

According to recent reports, liqid is also widening how customers buy memory pooling. At SC26, the tech giant announced Liqid as a Service, a fully managed, single-tenant offering, and it is moving toward preconfigured appliances. The bet is that most enterprises will deploy models rather than build them and therefore require their own capacity, according to Puri.

According to recent reports, “The world went to unlimited consumption of minutes, and that’s where we believe tokens are headed,” Puri mentioned. “Everybody’s going to own their own token machine so they can consume these tokens at will.”.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

In a recent development, bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

It has been revealed that almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

Industry observers note that this is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

Here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

It has been revealed that october’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also said a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

According to recent reports, and there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

According to recent reports, the risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets rapidly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Sources indicate that gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

In a recent development, the Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

On March 23, the Fed announced unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

According to recent reports, president Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

The response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Industry observers note that markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

The current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

Slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

The Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

The Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

In a recent development, at the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

But the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.
