Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put.
  • The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.
  • It has been revealed that the Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put. But helping free up housing in these districts isn't as simple as getting older people to move, a new study argues.

The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.

It has been revealed that the Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts. But it pinned that on affordability challenges. Higher-income households of all types compete for housing in the best-performing school districts.

Industry observers note that this is a conundrum for neighborhoods. Seniors are thus left in neighborhoods paying premiums for school districts they don't use. Meanwhile young families who'd like move into the district face limited options for homes there.

Of course, many seniors want to age in place in homes that they've lived in for decades. But others looking to downsize are "locked in" due to high mortgage rates. That can leave them in homes that they can't afford or, worse, in homes that pose safety risks for aging people.

"These findings suggest that policies aimed solely at encouraging older households to downsize are unlikely to substantially improve access to quality school districts," the paper claims.

Low housing turnover in these districts drives up prices. The higher-rated public school districts are, on average, 49% more expensive, and homes there move faster, Realtor.com® data shows. But in some of the nation's top school districts—including in Dallas, Los Angeles, and San Fransisco—homes can sell for three times the price of surrounding metros.

Using data from the American Community Survey, the Cleveland Fed found that households over 65 occupy a disproportionate share of the housing stock in the best-performing school districts. While these account for 26.2% of all households nationally, they make up as much as 28.7% of households in the least affordable areas.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile households with children, which make up about 31.2% of U.S. households, occupy 30.1% of housing in the best school districts and 40% of the housing stock in the lowest-quality districts. The same doesn't ring true for one-person households, which tend to be more evenly distributed.

Recent findings suggest that older homeowners move at about the same rate across all school districts—about 6.9% a year. About 81% of older adults in the best school districts own their homes. To the Cleveland Fed, that demonstrates older households aren't limiting turnover of housing stock in high-quality and high-cost districts.

It has been revealed that "While older households occupy a modestly larger share of housing in these expensive, high-quality areas, they do not appear to limit turnover," the paper states. "These patterns suggest that the challenge of accessing high-quality school districts is driven by a combination of income sorting and competition from multiple household types rather than solely by empty-nesters’ aging in place.".

Sources indicate that realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu says a few concerns are affecting seniors as they consider their futures. They include capital gains taxes they'd incur on homes that have appreciated in value. They also include the kinds of taxes they'd incur when they move to a new place. Then there are the social considerations.

Recent findings suggest that "Right-sized, single-level, accessible homes near family and doctors are scarce," Xu states. "Moving also means leaving behind the neighbors and community that owners have built over decades. For many longtime owners, there are few good places to go.".

Buyers can still find deals in some of these good markets, Realtor.com found, if they look carefully. But in some good districts, there simply aren't a lot of homes changing hands.

In a recent development, xu adds that she's surprised that young professionals without children can also compete for housing in these expensive districts. Jobs, urban amenities, and investment opportunity for the real estate tend to make these areas attractive.

Sources indicate that "Even if more seniors moved, the homes they left would likely go to higher-income buyers, because this is a sorting story. The districts wouldn’t become much more affordable," Xu states. "The more direct solution is building more homes in and near high-demand districts. Adding right-sized options could also give older owners who want to move somewhere to go, but supply is what would ease pressure on prices.".

To Arick Morton, CEO of NIC MAP, the frozen market points to a need for more housing oriented toward seniors. Earlier this year, his group said the nation needs to add 1 million upcoming senior housing units by 2040. That $1 trillion homebuilding frenzy would meet the moment 10 million baby boomers pass age 80.

It has been revealed that "People stay at home much longer than they did previously," Morton noted. "Of course folks stay at home as long as they can and then movie into senior housing when the need is there.".

But when there isn't enough senior housing or they don't have good alternatives to downsize, those seniors end up displaced when age or an accident means they require more intensive care needs.

"The best policy options are those that help expedite the construction of senior housing," Morton noted. "We don't have enough capacity to create a dent in that logjam.".

  • Memory bandwidth is a fundamental advantage that has to be solved,” Srivastava noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:21 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Sources indicate that as artificial intelligence workloads shift to inference, memory bandwidth decides whether hardware generates tokens rapidly or sits idle. D-Matrix Corp. is answering with Raptor, a second-generation chip stacking 3D DRAM beneath its compute logic.

AI infrastructure has become a systems game, and winners combine memory, interconnect and software into cohesive designs, according to Satyam Srivastava (pictured), fellow at d-Matrix.

“It’s no longer a chip problem. Chip plays a part of it. Memory bandwidth is a fundamental advantage that has to be solved,” Srivastava noted. “The next is energy efficiency. The next is interconnect efficiency. The next is software cohesiveness.”.

In a recent development, srivastava spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed d-Matrix’s Raptor chip and its stacked 3D DRAM, inference memory bandwidth and the shift toward heterogeneous computing. (* Disclosure below.).

In a recent development, D-Matrix proves each risky technology on a test chip first. Jayhawk proved die-to-die connectivity, and Jayhawk II validated digital in-memory computing. The Corsair accelerator combined both and entered full production earlier this year, Srivastava explained.

“Fast forward, we have the Pavehawk chip, test chip, which is proving out 3D DRAM stacked underneath the logic die, which serves as the core technology for Raptor, which is our second-generation chip coming out next year,” Srivastava said.

Stacking keeps the distributed memory architecture intact but moves memory cells onto a separate layer rather than consuming logic die area. Data travels a short distance and never crosses an interposer. That puts 3D DRAM in a upcoming tier between SRAM and high-bandwidth memory, Srivastava noted.

“So you’re getting 10 times higher energy efficiency compared to HBM, 10 times higher bandwidth compared to HBM, where it sits in between SRAM and HBM in terms of capacity,” Srivastava said.

According to recent reports, pairing a Corsair-based server with an existing Hopper GPU fleet can raise utilization from about 20% to as much as 80%, meaning more tokens per dollar, Srivastava noted. D-Matrix has also adopted NVLink Fusion rackscale infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. to connect its accelerators to Nvidia’s AI factories.

“For us, it unlocks the opportunity to participate in a very established ecosystem, the world’s most popular AI factory. We get access to a very hardened design of an MGX rack,” Srivastava remarked.

The partnership points toward heterogeneous computing, where software orchestrates GPUs, CPUs and accelerators such as Raptor as one system, with the cluster as the unit of computing, Srivastava explained.

“So think of a chip, but that chip is an entire cluster and it has many different hardware units,” Srivastava mentioned. “Some are GPUs, some are CPUs, some are ASIC accelerators, and you can use whichever one you like to serve the needs of the workload the best.”.

Breaking: Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hone Health, a physician-led virtual longevity care platform, has raised $228 million.
  • The investment is structured as a combination of equity and growth financing.
  • Hone will use the investment to support a number of expansions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hone Health, a physician-led virtual longevity care platform, has raised $228 million.

The investment is structured as a combination of equity and growth financing. The $28 million series A extension was led by MarcyPen Capital Partners, with participation from Pentland Ventures, Kinship Ventures, Hanwha, Gannet Capital, humbition and Comma Capital. Other angel investors also participated, including the Jonas brothers. The $200 million in growth financing came from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Hone will use the investment to support a number of expansions. It plans to launch more programming for metabolic health, PMOS, inflammation and immunity, and to launch a physician-supervised peptide program. It will add more diagnostics, including coronary CT angiography and gut microbiome analysis.

Hone also plans to continue building out its AI operating system that brings data together to help personalize care. And it plans to build out clinical trial infrastructure to support pharma partners.

“Longevity is thought of as this super exotic thing. […] I actually think longevity is now becoming primary care,” Saad Alam, co-founder and CEO of Hone, told Fierce Healthcare.

It has been revealed that it costs $65 to test for 70 biomarkers with Hone, followed by a clinician consult with the option to add more diagnostics. Labs, health history, symptoms and medications are run through its AI, which then gives providers treatment recommendations. Hone can keep adding additional diagnostics and medications, per Alam, “and the AI gets smarter as we get more patients into that system.”.

Additionally, Hone is publicly announcing Hone Black, a upcoming concierge longevity membership that has operated in stealth for a select group of patients for the past year. It combines diagnostics on over 1,600 health markers with ongoing medical care from physicians. Offerings include prescriptions, supplements, peptides and lifestyle guidance, plus exosome and stem cell therapies.

In a recent development, alam founded the company after experiencing a shift in his health at 35 years old, including mental health issues, depression and weight gain. His doctor was initially of little help. It took Alam a year to find out he had low testosterone, and after treatment, he finally felt back on track. That experience, along with his father dying from kidney disease and his mother going through early menopause, opened his eyes to the longevity space.

In a recent development, “This whole concept of longevity is going to be one of the single greatest problems I can dedicate my life to solving,” Alam realized at the time. He experimented with everything, from peptides to cold plunges to meditation.

Recent findings suggest that hone is a subsidiary of Time Therapeutics, which aims to support production of drugs that help people live longer. Alam, who started his career doing market research at Eli Lilly, knew clinical trials are expensive and inaccessible. He wanted to create a manufacturer that could help commercialize drugs. The first step to that is Hone, or a DTC virtual care company that can capture longitudinal data on patients. The next phase will be publishing research. Finally, Hone will look to partner with pharma to get drugs to market faster.

The company has been providing care for five years, treating about 200,000 patients to date. It requires patients to have a physician and get bloodwork every 90 days in order to get medication refills. Members can contact their clinician between sessions as needed.

“We make sure, for the most part, that you are doing bloodwork and talking to a physician, a real conversation with a physician, in order to get prescribed medication,” Alam noted.

It isn’t about overprescribing medications. It’s about finding the most personalized protocol for each patient. “The companies that have—no pun intended—longevity are the ones that are going to figure out how to reduce the number of medications somebody might need,” Alam stated.

According to recent reports, hone began with hormone therapy, then moved into longevity care with biomarker analysis and women’s health. Two months ago, Hone’s offerings for women surpassed offerings for men in terms of net new members. It soon aims to run clinical trials on poly-chronic patients as well to help determine the right drug at the right time. Hone crossed $100 million in revenue in 2025, per Alam, and is on track to double this year.

It has been revealed that “When I started goop, wellness was a niche conversation,” Gwyneth Paltrow, founder and CEO of goop and co-founder of Kinship Ventures, mentioned in a press release. “Today, it’s one of the biggest categories in the world, and the next step is bringing real health and wellness to the masses, not just the few. Saad has built Hone to do exactly that, with serious science and at real scale. That’s why Kinship invested, and we could not be more excited about what’s ahead.”.

Recent findings suggest that hone will soon offer 14 longevity care categories, which Alam argues is akin to primary care. He estimates that Hone only refers to in-person care about 10% of the time, usually for higher-acuity conditions. Some Hone patients are already healthy; most are sick and willing to pay out of pocket because the current system has been inadequate in solving their health needs, per Alam.

“This is just the beginning of not only a way but a complete change in the way that medicine is practiced,” Alam said. “A lot of other companies are what I’ll call pill mills, and where we’ve really focused—our energy is making sure that we go through the more difficult work of managing the long-term health of our patients.”.

A real-life Barbie dream house is turning heads in Hudson, WI, where an eye-catching pink Victorian has gone under contract after hitting the market for $1.1 million in June 2026.

With its pink walkway, bubble gum–colored staircase, and vibrant interior, this seven-bedroom, 5,189-square-foot home is anything but ordinary.

But behind its playful Barbie-inspired appearance is a spacious historical residence built in 1900 that is packed with character, original details, and incredible versatility.

“An everyday buyer interested in a classic Victorian home might think this is a bit much,” indicates listing agent Jennifer R. Martin of Edina Realty Inc. “It has a lot of great qualities. I would say to anyone not to let the color deter you. Painting is easy, and it’s not that expensive to make changes.”.

Currently a successful short-term rental, the home is near the St. Croix River and could be used for multigenerational living or converted into a single-family home.

Industry observers note that “The sizing alone of the house is incredible,” Martin notes. “It’s enormous and goes on forever. It has two separate kitchens, so it could also be turned into a duplex.”.

It is part of a collection of rose-hued homes operated by Fleetwood Rentals, which hosts everything from birthday parties to bachelorette weekends.

It has been revealed that “The seller’s clientele is looking for a party weekend destination,” she notes. “It’s one block from the riverfront and two blocks away from downtown.”.

According to recent reports, located 30 minutes from the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport, the property last changed hands for $614,000 in 2020. It offers “outstanding income potential,” the listing states.

“When the seller bought it, right away she had it painted in dark charcoal,” Martin states. “Her vision at that time was to have a Goth mansion that would be similar to Disney’s Haunted Mansion. It was right around the time the 'Barbie' movie was coming out, so she decided to take advantage of that.”.

Recent findings suggest that the multilevel home also has formal and casual dining spaces and expansive gathering areas. Original details include woodwork, built-in cabinetry, vaulted ceilings, and dual staircases.

"I envisioned the next buyer to be either another Airbnb owner or a large family who would un-pinkify it," Martin says with a laugh. "It's a great house with a lot of great qualities. I told potential buyers not to let the color deter you.".

The living room has pink walls, drapes, and couches. The formal dining room has built-in cabinetry and a fireplace. The light-filled kitchen, with an enormous breakfast bar, is a surprise with its white cabinetry and a copper farmhouse sink.

Industry observers note that the bubble gum–painted grand staircase leads to the colorful sleeping quarters. Four bedrooms are on the second level and three more are on the third floor. The primary suite has a walk-in closet, a soaking tub, a separate glass shower, and a dual-sink vanity.

Other highlights include a home theater, a hot tub, a 14-foot swim spa, and a patio designed for entertaining. The fenced lot comes with a private patio, a two-car garage, and a driveway with parking for 12 vehicles.

The property is conveniently located near boutique shopping, riverfront parks, and the marina.

"Hudson is a riverfront town with tons of history," Martin claims. "People love to come here for bachelorette parties and places to go out to dinner. It also has a lot of charming, fun shops.".

HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers roll out peptide offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Direct-to-consumer health companies Noom and Hims & Hers are making a play for the peptide market as the federal government loosens restrictions on compounded treatments.

The companies are betting that peptides could be the next big thing in consumer health. For Noom, the upcoming peptide offering extends the organization's business beyond weight loss into the broader longevity and wellness market. Hims & Hers signaled months ago that it was ready to tap into the multi-billion-dollar peptide market.

In a recent development, federal policy shifts and U.S. Food and Drug Administration enforcement discretion around compounded peptides have opened new pathways for telehealth and compounding pharmacies.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, Noom introduced OpenRx as a separate peptide and preventive health brand. At launch, OpenRx offers two injectable options: sermorelin, a peptide frequently prescribed for muscle support, and NAD+, a coenzyme frequently prescribed for energy. OpenRx also offers two oral dissolvable tablet options: the first formulation combines the peptides PT-141 and oxytocin with tadalafil to support sexual health. The second ODT formulation is the peptide oxytocin to support intimacy.

Industry observers note that noom indicates it plans to expand into other areas including recovery, muscle health, skin, gut health and sleep. Peptides are small pieces of protein that occur naturally in the body and help control functions such as growth, healing and appetite.

According to recent reports, “Peptides are an important portion of the formulary of healthy aging,” Geoff Cook, CEO of Noom, stated in a statement. “OpenRx enables our flagship Noom brand to deepen into cardiometabolic health while the new brand OpenRx supports patients with conditions too often neglected by traditional care models, like energy, muscle composition, skin health, sexual health, sleep, and recovery. Together, both brands support the same mission: to empower everyone, everywhere to live better longer – every day.”.

Industry observers note that noom claims every OpenRx prescription is written by a licensed clinician following an evaluation of the patient’s health history, goals and clinical appropriateness. Treatments are fulfilled through Noom’s U.S.-based pharmacy network, which operates under state boards of pharmacy oversight and adheres to USP compounding standards, the company noted.

In a recent development, noom is right now reviewing BPC-157 and TB-500 as part of its ongoing process of evaluating emerging treatments for inclusion in our formulary, Jeffrey Egler, M.D., Noom's chief medical officer, said in a statement. "Each therapy offered by OpenRx is selected because our clinical team and I believe it is appropriate for improving patient health. The process involves continuous monitoring of safety-related signals, gathering the judgment of our medical directors and the medical directors of affiliated clinical networks based on years of prescribing experience with the compounds in question, ensuring a compliant and stable supply chain, sourcing of active pharmaceutical ingredients, and setting up processes for compliance with state and federal adverse event reporting guidelines," Egler said.

It has been revealed that online health and wellness brand Hims & Hers announced earlier this month it planned to roll out a peptides business. As part of the tech giant's new Peptides+ specialty, introduced today, it plans to initially sell five U.S.-compounded peptide and longevity treatments—Sermorelin, NAD+, Glutathione, Vitamin B12 and L-Carnitine, with plans to add more peptides and therapies over time.

The company also plans to offer U.S.-made BPC-157 and TB-500 "consistent with regulatory requirements," the company remarked.

A survey the company conducted in October of 2,000 adults found that more than half (55%) said they were interested in or curious about peptide therapies, and 40% of U.S. adults say they are interested or very interested in a telehealth offering of injectable prescription treatments, including peptides and other compounded treatments. Nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults (9%) say they currently use peptides, not including FDA-approved peptides such as Ozempic, Wegovy and insulin, the survey found.

In a recent development, peptides are in the spotlight due to the massive success of FDA-approved GLP-1 weight loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which are peptide drugs. Wellness influencers and biohackers on social media are promoting other lab-made peptides for fast-tracked healing, anti-aging and muscle growth.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has championed looser federal rules on trendy, unapproved peptide injections. In July, an FDA advisory committee recommended broader access to six unapproved peptides. The panel recommended adding these six substances to the Section 503A Bulks List, which would remove the restrictions on how they are produced by compounders, Fierce Pharma reported.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Kennedy has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued in late October, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

But medical experts have raised safety and clinical evidence questions around unapproved or experimental compounds. The American Medical Association (AMA) publicly opposes the Trump administration’s initiative to make certain unapproved peptides more widely available for human use.

In a letter (PDF) to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the AMA pushed back what it called a "rushed" decision to permit the compounding of certain peptides because they have not been approved for safe use by the FDA.

Unproven peptides may pose serious health risks, including allergic reactions, infections, hormonal imbalances and other unexpected side effects, according to the FDA website.

"We should not bypass the science and put patients at risk by making them guinea pigs for unapproved drugs," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement. "If these substances are safe and effective, the evidence should demonstrate that through the FDA’s rigorous review process.".

Hims & Hers' peptide therapy program provides a "clinically guided, personalized plan" for consumers "backed by a licensed provider who understands these therapies," according to Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., chief medical officer of the Hims brand.

Hims & Hers wants to "set the standard" for peptide therapy and offer consistency in the quality of the products, Vinjamoori said in an interview on the sidelines of the HLTH conference this week.

"If you think about what we have to bring to the table with our scale and resources, I would argue there's no one better equipped to do it than us," Vinjamoori remarked.

Hims & Hers has invested in its supply chain and expanded its domestic manufacturing facilities. In 2025, the organization acquired a Menlo Park peptide facility to run API validation and stability testing to support its specialized peptide offerings.

"That's why we're investing in our supply chain and doing a lot of the hard work that, frankly, is not the fastest path to making these available. There are pharmacies that are already out there that are making these available, and there are companies out there that will simply just plug into those pharmacies and service patients. But there are inconsistencies," he noted.

According to recent reports, until now, getting these types of medications has often meant relying on unreliable and unregulated online sellers, or a high-cost longevity clinic, Hims & Hers executives said. Hims & Hers' peptides offering gives consumers more accessible care, "backed by real medical leadership and with consistent clinical oversight," the company said in a press release.

Hims & Hers believes its scale gives it an opportunity and responsibility to help build the evidence base around peptides, using growing patient interest not just to expand access but to better understand how the treatments can be used safely and effectively, Vinjamoori said.

Recent findings suggest that expanding into peptides fits with Hims & Hers' ongoing focus on personalized health, he noted. "We started with sexual health, moved on to hair loss, and then we've continued to broaden into other categories such as hormone replacement, GLP-1s, and now peptides, and many others to come. And the common theme in all of this is that we're talking about helping people accomplish a specific goal that they have. We're not talking about curing a disease or treating a disease per se," he remarked. "We're talking about, 'Hey, there's something you want to do in your life that you're not able to do right now. Let's help you figure out how we can put together a proposal to help you accomplish that.".

According to recent reports, "This is a big part of the future of medicine itself," Vinjamoori added. "It's been the missing part of the equation, where we've been very focused on treating and responding to disease, but not as much, not just on prevention, but really on helping people use their health as an asset and as a tool to help them accomplish what they want in life.".

Industry observers note that with Hims & Hers' peptide therapy offering, consumers start with a clinical visit with a licensed provider that includes a comprehensive intake of health history and goals. The company said a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies assesses each individual and, if appropriate, tailors a personalized protocol to their needs.

It has been revealed that hims & Hers treatments are compounded in the U.S. and dispensed directly by licensed, U.S. pharmacies regulated by state boards of pharmacy and "held to rigorous quality and safety standards," the manufacturer said.

The buzz around peptides ties into consumers' growing interest in taking control of their health "driven by the cultural zeitgeist moment," Vinjamoori told Fierce Healthcare.

Recent findings suggest that "There's a variety of different factors that catalyze that. I think the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a lot of it for a variety of reasons. I think you see accelerations in biotechnology where people now see something like GLP-1s that can help with a problem that seemed intractable before. I think people are now interested in figuring out what is the range of solutions that could help me. I also think peptides represent something that has a lot of promise, a lot of excitement," he mentioned.

"But there are also some cautions that we need to take as well. Something we think a lot about is how do we meet this moment of excitement and enthusiasm with some degree of rigor and guardrails," Vinjamoori noted.

Sources indicate that "It starts with the product itself. How do we ensure the quality? The compounds are of the highest quality and are compounded in the most rigorous way, made available in the most rigorous way. That's why we are trying to have as much oversight as we can into the full process of making these available," he said.

Industry observers note that he asserted that informed consent and transparency with consumers are critical. "I've spent a lot of time with the team to make sure that we understand that people have this enthusiasm, but we need to make sure that they understand what they're getting into. There is a difference between this and FDA-approved therapies," he said.

According to recent reports, "Sometimes people should try the standard of care before they engage with some of these things, and so we want to make sure we have these conversations with people openly and honestly. But at the same time, we also want to respect their choice," he added.

Sources indicate that hims & Hers Peptides+ is available with its Care+ program that gives customers access to twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress, unlimited support and ongoing check-ins from a dedicated care team. Customers can also message providers trained in peptide therapy 24/7 with any questions. The Hims Men’s panel includes at-home blood collection and access to lab tests that provide insights across 22 biomarkers, including testosterone, vitamin D, and cholesterol. The Hers Women’s panel tests 22 biomarkers across hormones, vitamins, and heart health.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, as AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead.
  • Sources indicate that “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:29 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

In a recent development, as AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

Sources indicate that “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”.

Industry observers note that botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.).

“Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”.

For enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the tech giant’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija noted. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a organization.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act.
  • Senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.

Sources indicate that the Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act. Much of that was aimed at substantial energy infrastructure, but it also has implications for housing and even data centers.

Senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill. It's since been attached to a larger and more popular bill, but lawmakers have been debating and tweaking it for several weeks.

Recent findings suggest that the latest version released this month updated language to assuage concerns that it would weaken environmental protections and rights of Native American groups. The bill has been popular but divisive: While the speed would boost green energy like wind and solar power, plus electric infrastructure that lowers costs, it could also speed along fossil fuel investments, like natural gas pipelines, and nuclear power.

Recent findings suggest that "Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs," Lee stated on the floor before the vote. The bill could make "everything you buy" less expensive in the long run.

Industry observers note that but several housing advocates have cheered the bill, saying it would make it easier to build affordable housing and invest in local communities. They include the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, the Niskanen Center, Associated Builders and Contractors, and the National Community Development Association.

"America’s housing shortage demands solutions that make it easier and more affordable to build," National Association of Realtors® Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn said. NAR "supports streamlining permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction, and limit housing supply.".

Industry observers note that A White House policy paper estimates federal permitting requirements for major infrastructure take 4.2 years to complete—and produce 1,700 pages of paperwork. It expects reforms to increase the GDP by $82 billion to $164 billion and produce $14 billion to $28 billion in tax revenue.

It also remarked permitting reform could cut electric bills by $178 to $251 a year for the average household. President Donald Trump urged the bill's passage in a post on Truth Social, calling it "a MASSIVE WIN.".

"This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs," the president posted.

"We can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs," Whitehouse mentioned.

A number of groups opposed to the bill argued that some of the protections it removes would endanger protections for Native American groups and hamstring environmental preservation.

Recent findings suggest that the Association on American Indian Affairs noted the bill would "threaten Native sovereignty and the protections that safeguard our country's cultural and historic heritage." The Endangered Species Coalition claims it would weaken protections. Both continued to oppose the bill even as it was amended.

The House would need to vote on the bill next, and members have already began debating its merits.

"Even as amended, it undermines Tribal sovereignty, environmental laws, and locks in dangerous projects," Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-NM) remarked in an X post. "This is NOT the deal, NOT the time, and NOT what the American people asked for.".

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) cast the bill as a way for Republicans to use the remaining weeks of their majority to improve affordability for Americans.

It has been revealed that "One of the biggest things we can do to address affordability for the long term is to ensure a reliable and affordable energy supply," Thune said. “And that starts with ensuring that energy projects don’t face unnecessary permitting barriers.".

The federal permitting process, he later remarked, "has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations.

“And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death," Thune mentioned. “We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges.".

A poll by moderate think tank Third Way found bipartisan support for the tenets of the bill. About 62% of respondents named lowering utility bills as a top concern, and 57% keeping the power grid reliable.

“It’s more notable than ever to pass permitting reform this year. The overwhelming support for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act reflects the Senate’s commitment to addressing the nation's energy affordability challenges.".

The bill was also host to Congress' latest effort to rein in data center developments proliferating throughout the country. One amendment by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) would have banned data centers on public lands. Republicans blocked it.

"There is enormous concern that this bill puts the pedal to the floor on data centers across the country," Wyden remarked on the floor.

In a recent development, following Democrats' gains in the House after the 2026 midterms, a number of left-leaning groups have called for a hesitant Congress to formulate more laws involving data centers. Among them, the Chamber of Progress called for federal AI safety standards and requirements for data centers to cover their own costs.

A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also mentioned that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

Industry observers note that but that doesn't mean they don't affect communities. A group of Senate Democrats, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, released a report pinning other costs on them. It also criticized the tax incentives.

"This investigation finds the data center industry is bulldozing local communities and using their economic resources to play states and local communities against one another, creating a race to the bottom in which state and local policymakers feel they have no choice but to accede to the data centers’ demands—and leaving ordinary citizens stuck with the bills," they noted in a joint statement.

Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. Virginia spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. Ohio lost $2 billion in foregone revenue from its incentive in two years alone.

HLTH 2026: Viz.ai’s chief clinical officer on takeaways, goals of AI collab with National Rural Health Association" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It’s been almost seven months since artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform Viz.ai entered into a partnership with the National Rural Health Association (NRHA).

The partnership aims to help rural healthcare leaders better understand and implement AI tools across systems. That's been a personal and professional passion of Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim, M.D., who discussed with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH his key takeaways from the collaboration thus far and forward-looking goals as it approaches its one-year mark.

In a recent development, ibrahim said that the two organizations have done three educational events for rural health systems since the partnership kicked off in April. These series aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI—and whether they should adopt it, he said.

He noted there’s “sometimes a very major mismatch” when smaller rural health systems onboard multiple vendors.

“We've learned [that] many rural hospitals don't have the IT expertise and infrastructure to adopt some of these tools, and so it's actually been a force function to strengthen their hub spoke relationships,” Ibrahim remarked.

Strengthening these relationships, according to Ibrahim, has been key.

“It's actually been beautiful to see the hub-spoke relationship strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit,” Ibrahim said. “And it gives them a reason to interact more, and a way for the rural hospitals to strengthen their capabilities.”.

He continued, “there's an authenticity about the moment where it's like ‘Yeah, we do need to help each other out.’ We're all kind of figuring it out as we go.”.

In addition to the educational series, Ibrahim said frameworks are in development to aid rural health systems in navigating, implementing and deploying AI—which will be built into a toolkit.

One of Ibrahim’s personal goals for the one-year mark of the partnership is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when pitched.

“I think that would be a huge milestone,” he noted. “Getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal—probably unrealistic, but that's probably the ultimate goal.”.

And when it comes to metrics for measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim stated he's looking for numbers that show participants are “keeping more care local” and retaining their workforces.

“It would be great to be able to connect the dots [and understand whether] adoption of an AI tool give[s] rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm, willingness to stay in their community as opposed to dropping the services and moving back,” he said.

Another initiative from Viz that has “disproportionate benefit in rural communities,” according to Ibrahim, is its new partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

“I'm pretty excited about being able to bring their level of clinical decision support into our rural hospitals,” he said.

Jon Hamm and Anna Osceola are officially parents! The "Your Friends & Neighbors" co-stars welcomed their first child together.

The upcoming bundle of joy is a boy, according to a People magazine source.

The couple, who met on the set of "Mad Men," first sparked speculation that they were expecting after Osceola, 38, was seen with a baby bump during a trip to the Hamptons—with sources quickly confirming to People magazine that Hamm, 55, and his spouse were happily preparing to welcome a child.

The actor—who tied the knot to Osceola in an intimate cliffside ceremony in California in 2023—broke his silence on those rumors during an appearance on “Late Night With Seth Meyers," telling Meyers that he was "very excited and deeply terrified" about becoming a dad.

“I think I’m doing it right," he mentioned, adding that those feelings shouldn't ever “go away.”.

He then poked fun at his age, teasing, "When your kid is 70, you’ll be like, ‘I did it!’ When I’m 152.”.

According to recent reports, back when rumors began surfacing that the couple was expecting, an unnamed insider told People, “Jon’s incredibly excited. This is something he and Anna have wanted and hoped for. He’s not thinking about his age or what anyone else has to say about it. He’s just really happy.”.

The source added that Hamm is "happy, settled, and ready" for the next stage of his life, while a different insider told Us Weekly that the couple was "trying to relax a bit but are enjoying making plans for the baby.".

While the process of nesting can look entirely different from one family to the next, the news about Hamm and Osceola's fresh addition does raise a question about whether the couple will raise the baby in the actor's longtime $4 million Los Feliz pad, which he purchased in 2017, before he was officially linked with his now-wife.

Though the home served as a bachelor pad for Hamm for several years, it has since become a marital residence for the couple and could now evolve once again—this time, into a family dwelling.

Certainly the four-bedroom, 3,600-square-foot home boasts plenty of room for a family of three. There's a spacious kitchen equipped with top-of-the-line appliances and a spacious pantry.

The 4.5 bathrooms feature spa-worthy furnishings, while the comfortable family room opens up to a stunning backyard patio complete with a built-in grill station, fire pit, and saltwater pool.

The property’s midcentury aesthetic makes it the kind of place one might picture the actor’s most notable on-screen character, Don Draper, residing, with wood paneling and asymmetrical design choices that ooze character while maintaining a peaceful environment.

The gated property is located at the end of a charming cul-de-sac in the Los Angeles neighborhood, which many big names in Hollywood have called home over the years, including Brad Pitt, Kristen Wiig, and Aubrey Plaza.

It’s not the first time Hamm has invested in the area, purchasing a 3,100-square-foot Los Feliz abode for $900,000 in 2002 with his then-partner, actress Jennifer Westfeldt. The duo parted ways in 2015 after spending 18 years together.

During his previous relationship, Hamm was not sold on the concept of fatherhood.

“I see my friends who have children and I’m like, ‘Dude, how are you even upright, much less here at work at 6 a.m.?” he candidly mentioned to Us in 2012.

However, he’s changed his tune since beginning a life with Osceola and is now “over the moon” at the thought of enjoying a fresh life as a dad, according to an Us Weekly source.

“Jon has always wanted to be a dad with Anna,” the source continued. “Having a family was something that was really crucial to both of them from the beginning.

"They’ve talked about this chapter for a long time and were always on the same page about wanting children, so for it to be actually happening now feels incredibly special.”.

The Emmy-winning performer has opened up about his desire to have a family with his wife, telling The Hollywood Reporter that, due to his parents’ divorce during his childhood, he “didn’t look at marriage as a thing,” but was hopeful for his own union to turn into a growing family.

“I will be the old dad, but so it goes,” he stated in 2024, then 53 years old. “It could be a good thing. We’ll see.”.

Hamm and Osceola first crossed paths in 2015, when filming the finale episode of “Mad Men” in Substantial Sur, CA.

In a recent development, romance rumors swirled in 2017, but their relationship was not officially confirmed until 2020. The couple made their public red carpet debut at the Vanity Fair Oscars Party in 2022.

Hamm eventually popped the question. “I just knew at a certain point I wanted to be with this person,” he shared with The Hollywood Reporter in 2023. “But when I proposed, I was terrified. I was like, ‘What am I doing?’”.

The couple tied the knot in July 2023, with their sentimental wedding celebration serving as a thoughtful nod to their “Mad Men” roots.

The ceremony was held at Anderson Canyon, the Big Sur spot where they first met when filming the show’s final episode. Surrounded by loved ones and lush florals, they exchanged vows alongside the Pacific Ocean.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Industry observers note that the U.S. Department of Labor proposed newly introduced policy this week that would end fast-track green cards for healthcare professionals like nurses and physical therapists—the latest in a string of policies from the Trump administration raising the bar for foreign-born workers and students across healthcare and other industries.

Presently, nurses, physical therapists and other workers “with exceptional ability in the sciences or arts” are granted an exemption from an administrative test in the permanent labor certification program (PERM), a months-long administrative process in which an employer must prove there are no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers for a permanent job ahead of sponsoring a foreign worker.

Sources indicate that the exemption, referred to Schedule A, is given to occupations where the DOL recognizes a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers. Nurses and physical therapists have been listed under Schedule A for more than 30 years.

The Department of Labor, in its newly proposed rule, said it wants to eliminate Schedule A as it cannot “demonstrate that the occupations at the moment listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations.”.

It cited in the proposed rule a late 2023 request for information published under the Biden administration seeking input on potentially expanding Schedule A. Despite more than 2,000 responses, DOL now says it didn’t receive the information it would need to establish a methodology for regularly reviewing and updating Schedule A occupations, and questioned whether it has the statutory authority to make such occupational exemptions in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that “The elimination of Schedule A would enable the Department to better ensure that U.S. workers have an opportunity to apply for available job opportunities, and adhere to the statutory requirements to protect U.S. workers assigned to it, as intended by Congress under the [Immigration and Nationality Act].”.

The proposed rule, which is open to public comment for 60 days, also includes requirements for employers to advertise their open jobs more broadly and for a longer period of time to demonstrate a good-faith effort to recruit American workers before turning to a green card sponsorship. These and other proposed changes would be the first “comprehensive” reforms to the PERM program in almost two decades, the Department of Labor remarked.

If finalized as-is, employers who want to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and other affected roles “would be required to go through the lengthier and costlier PERM labor market testing process, adding time, cost and administrative work to a pathway that hospitals, nursing homes and rehabilitation providers have historically relied on to fill persistent shortages,” Caroline Tang, an Austin shareholder at labor and employment law firm Ogletree Deakins, told Fierce Healthcare.

In a recent development, industry associations as well as other sections of the government have widely projected shortages in the healthcare workforce, including nurses, for the coming years. The Heart Resources and Services Association’s National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, for instance, projects (PDF) national shortages of registered nurses through at least 2038, with a projected 8% shortage in 2028 that is more severe in non-metro areas.

The proposed policy change is among several brought by the Trump administration in line with an order from the White House to prioritize domestic hiring—though many have been stymied in the courts.

According to recent reports, among the most prominent is a $100,000 supplemental fee the Department of Homeland Security attached to H-1B petitions that was vacated by two separate judged, and in August was succeeded by the somewhat altered proposal of an additional H-1B petition fee of $103,265. Another policy from the same department tightening how long nonimmigrant students may remain in the country (referred to as “duration of status”) was temporary blocked hours before implementation in September and fully vacated on Monday (PDF), though the former decision is already being appealed.

The Department of Labor has also proposed increasing the prevailing wage floors for several green cards that legal experts expect will be challenged by employers that would shoulder the resulting financial burden.

#122148. What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2902 w)

What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.
  • Sources indicate that revenue more than doubled year-over-year.
  • Industry observers note that this was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was revealed on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:32 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Sources indicate that nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Sources indicate that revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the organization’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

Industry observers note that this was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was revealed on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the manufacturer’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly noted he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”.

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The tech giant made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress remarked the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Industry observers note that asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Sources indicate that employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the tech giant held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress declared plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

Recent findings suggest that for information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

Industry observers note that one of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he mentioned the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our latest CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”.

That was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued upcoming export controls this week, which the manufacturer “still has some time to study.”.

Recent findings suggest that huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

Industry observers note that for IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The upcoming Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

With demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

Sources indicate that “All are getting the same pricing,” Kress stated. “That is super key for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”.

Recent findings suggest that those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress remarked the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

The lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so quickly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain notable, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She noted Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”.

According to recent reports, two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

“Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still prepares to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”.

This was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

According to recent reports, the flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

Industry observers note that my advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

The demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress remarked agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

The CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive new spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress stated, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom shows how rapidly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

The network is part of this, too. Kress remarked co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, declared at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, initiative CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

The question of who the new CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the company.

Recent findings suggest that most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip tech giant, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

Industry observers note that the next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:.

Recent findings suggest that matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves promptly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Recent findings suggest that charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management company. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Sources indicate that two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

Also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the organization can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an important hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

Sources indicate that this call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current plans and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

In a recent development, zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.
  • The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov.
  • Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac.

Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.

It has been revealed that so what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

In a recent development, at today's 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,354. This reflects a $40 monthly increase from the previous week’s payment of $2,314.

Compared to the 6.26% average from November 2025, which required a $2,120 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $234 more a month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,839.

This reflects a $48 increase from last week's monthly cost of $2,791. Compared to the 6.26% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,558, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $281 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $145 in relief.

The long-term financial picture highlights how this abrupt reversal affects total borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.28% rate will pay a total of $847,328 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While this week's jump erased much of the ground gained over the past month, this total still represents a contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $43,302 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

According to recent reports, FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.28% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,022,090 for principal and interest.

Sources indicate that if that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $52,233 for FHA buyers.

UnitedHealthcare's new care model leans on community pharmacies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealthcare is teaming up with CPSEN for a upcoming program that will lean on community pharmacists to reach Medicaid patients.

The insurance giant remarked Wednesday that its through the UHC Pharmacy Care Hub model, pharmacists will work alongside the payer's care managers and providers to help close gaps in care and support management for chronic conditions and other needs.

Sources indicate that participating pharmacies will offer a range of services, including telehealth, medication management, point-of-care testing and personalized supports. The program is built on a hub-and-spoke model, where pharmacists can then help lead the patient to the right site of care or through any follow-up if needed.

These interactions can also help track patterns in emergency care use, and help patients find a more appropriate setting if their needs aren't emergent.

The program is right now available to UnitedHealthcare Medicaid members in seven states: Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. UHC expects to add additional states throughout the year.

Part of the goal, the manufacturer said, is to tap into the trust that local pharmacists have in the communities they serve.

Industry observers note that “Community pharmacies are trusted, local access points for care,” said Arethusa Kirk, M.D., chief medical officer for UnitedHealthcare Community & State, in the announcement. “This latest model expands the services independent pharmacists can help deliver, making it easier for people—especially those facing barriers to care—to get timely support closer to home.”.

UHC noted that most (89%) of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy, making these locations an easier option to access for many. This is especially true for individuals who may struggle to find an appointment with a doctor or find transportation to a visit.

For example, a participating pharmacist in North Carolina, Madeline Clark, said in the announcement that a patient came into the pharmacy for a urine test, as she had a potential urinary tract infection. The pharmacy conducted the test and sent the results virtually to a provider through UnitedHealthcare's Doctor Chat tool.

A prescription was then filled for the patient in the same visit, and she was out the door within about 30 minutes.

Clark said the patient was thankful not just for the ease of that trip to the pharmacy but for avoiding a visit to the ER as well.

"Not only was this a lower cost of care in the healthcare system space, but it also was just incredibly helpful for the patient," she noted.
